items.body:
In the 15+ years that have elapsed since 'Loop Finding Jazz Records' first shuffled out of his ambrosially dusty speakers, Jan Jelinek's most famous album has acquired an almost mythical status. Originally released via Pole's defunct Scape imprint, it now finds new life via Jelinek's own Faitiche label, for a new generation to marvel at one of the finest examples of loop-based electronic music typical of the early noughties.

Taking what reads like a pretty austere set of ingredients, Jelinek's technique revolves around a trio of elements which consist of second long cuts of 1960's-70's jazz recordings, the loop-finding modulation wheel (do your homework!) and the Moiré effect; albeit rendered in the acoustic as opposed to the image and spectral domains.

If all this sounds a bit academic, be assured that on record it is anything but; as crumbling edifices of mealy rhythms slowly pulse into life and swirl around your head like snow storms clashing with a dust devil. Taking sediments of fathom deep static then skimming the best stuff from the top, Jelinek opens through the dampened echoes of 'Moiré (piano & organ)' wherein a slow-motion thrum of spiraling clicks, rustles and analogue tones conspire to give the impression of recondite perspectives that extend well beyond the constituent elements.

Elsewhere, 'Rocky in the Video Age' instills a gratuitously optimistic blush to the aquatic micro-sound ebb, 'Moiré (Strings)' is a perfect companion to Basinski's disintegrating tape archive, whilst 'Them, Their' represents an aural crease so sleight you can only catch its distinctive gleam from the corner of your eye.

items.body:
Living legend of Berlin dub, Paul St. Hilaire aka Tikiman (Rhythm & Sound) is subject of a much-needed retrospective scanning solo productions across three decades for Kynant Records.

Adored around these parts for his ohrwurm vox as Tikiman on Rhythm & Sound’s Burial Mix records, Paul St. Hilaire is a Dominican artist based in Berlin since the ‘90s, where he’s honed a singular style of dub finely balanced between Caribbean tradition and its European offshoots. Any Berlin dub fiend will tell you, however, that St. Hilaire’s work does not stop at Rhythm & Sound, with his dulcet baritone also key to recordings by a raft of related artists such as René Löwe (Vainqueur), Deadbeat, and Rhauder, not to mention Larry Heard and Modeselektor. Perhaps lesser known are St. Hilaire’s inimitable solo productions, as previously showcased on a pair of albums for his False Tuned label, and now in abundance on ‘Tikiman Vol.1’, which reels between meditative steppers, psych-dub, rolling house and drowsy lovers for a rare insight to his cloud chamber studio floating somewhere above Kreuzberg.

While the tunes may bear a striking similarity to Rhythm & Sound, it’s all St. Hilaire’s own productions, custom-built with an extensive collection of vintage hardware to accompany his “patois metaphors on education, displacement and personal vs. global histories.” Reflecting on life between Dominica and Berlin, and especially as as one of the city’s long-standing but scant number of Black artists, it supplies a unique skew on the german capital’s beloved dub house/techno sound. Between the smoked-out dub blooz of ‘Bedroom in My Bag’ and the waves of rolling dub noise clag to ‘Three and a Half’, he echoes timeless work with Rhythm & Sound in the deep lovers dub mystery of ‘Little Way’ and ‘Keep Safe’, coining mesmerising sort of dub poetry on ‘Bright One’ and giving dancers something to trot to with the elegant pressure of ‘The Weather Man’, the swollen bass of ‘Ten To One’, and his skanking dub-jazz-house ace ‘In Door’. Legend.

items.body:
Sferic/Faitiche emissary Roméo Poirier pairs up with stylistic mentor Jan Jelinek on a sampler's delight, answering Jelinek's romantic 2005 gem 'Collage of Digital Passion' with a montaged mirror image that fizzes with plunderphonic warmth.

Jelinek has been using The Exposures pseudonym since 2003, most notably pillaging micro-samples from numerous R&B records on "Collage Of Digital Passion” issued by Prefuse 73’s Eastern Developments label back in 2005. In his by-now inimitable loop-finding style, that track has become a bit of a low-slung classic, reminding us not only of his iconic productions of the early 2000’s, but also of Anthony Shakir’s iconic ‘Mr. Shakir's Beat Store’ from just a couple of years earlier.

For his “version”, Poirier flips “I hate you!" samples with fanciful, theatrical soundscapes that ooze warmth, capturing the essence of Jelinek's original perfectly.

items.body:
Trust when we say that Anderson do Paraiso has made one of the deadliest albums we’ve heard this year (pick a year, any will do), a genius session of no-drums Grimey madness from Belo Horizonte that’s emblematic of Brazil’s fiercely innovative new wave of producers, making it our number 2 album of the year, 2023.

The most unsettlingly brilliant music we've heard yet from Brazil, Anderson do Paraiso's 'Queridão' strips favela funk down to its barest bones, interspersing raps and hooks with slowed down flutes, strings, metallic prangs, drill basslines and fritzed folk samples, pulling propulsion from seemingly nowhere. 

"I want it to be dark. The darker the better," Anderson told Brazilian magazine Volume Morto in 2020. The producer taught himself to make beats in 2012, but when he started attending the Baile de Serrão, a street party in Belo Horizonte's largest favela, his sound immediately shifted, pairing MC’s rapping about sexual liaisons and drugs with an increasingly slower, more haunted and screwed no-drums backing. The sound became known as funk BH or funk mineiro, and Anderson became one of its most notorious producers.

If you heard DJ K's 'Panico No Submundo' from earlier this year, it's worth noting that his bruxaria funk variant, while still cripplingly dark, exists on the other side of the spectrum. If DJ K propels his blown-out beats towards the carnival's haunted house, Anderson instead aims his sights at a dimly-lit dungeon, watching his pace like a hawk and adding percussive blocks only when absolutely necessary. That sparse production allows the MCs' idiosyncrasies to jump out, often pairing stark raps and hooks over loose violin phrases, an occasional kickdrum and sharp, metallic percussion. His skill lies in using space to galvanise the mood, tightly delaying the vocals where necessary and letting the gaps create a paralysing level of tension.  A familiar beat might make an occasional appearance, but Anderson keeps it bare and alien, weaving in chuckles and off-key piano instead of fastening himself to the formula.

At its best, the record sounds like the haunted memory of music that at one point may have been more full and chaotic, sometimes adding slippery synths and rousing trumpets, at others lathering up layers of pitchy vocal loops and orgasmic moans. ‘On CHAMAS SUAS COLEGAS PRA BRINCAR' -  the album's most pitch-black cut - Anderson takes monastic chorals and church bells, creating a kind of aesthetic dissonance that’s pretty much like nothing else we’ve heard.

Effortlessly experimental and fully gripping throughout, 'Queridão' is one of the most abstract and inspiring dance records we've heard this year, boasting vocal performances and production that'll have you hitting repeat again and again just to work out what the hell’s going on. It's exactly what we've been waiting for - grab it before the vultures start picking at its bones.

items.body:
Clocking in at over four hours (!), 'Giant Beauty' documents a five night performance from pianist Pat Thomas, bassist Joel Grip, drummer Antonin Gerbal and saxophonist Seymour Wright, who barrel through the canon of under-appreciated US jazz innovator Ahmed Abdul-Malik. Seriously physical, transcendent material, it's crucial listening for anyone intrigued by the fertile space between hard bop, free jazz, Arabic music and West African modes.

Abdul-Malik was a complex, quietly inspiring figure who impressed his interest in West Asian Islamic cultures and Afican musics onto the mutable framework of hard bop. A prodigious multi-instrumentalist who could play violin, tuba, bass, piano and cello, he'd come up in Brooklyn, playing bass with various ensembles while he was barely out of high school. And when he converted to Islam, he dedicated himself to understanding the culture on a deeper level, learning Arabic fluently and experimenting with instruments such as the oud and the qanun. During the 1950s Abdul-Malik's notoriety grew significantly thanks to his tenure playing with hard bop legend Art Blakey, but he was creatively undernourished, desperate to find a way to integrate the sounds he was hearing from New York's Arab community into jazz. So after working with Thelonious Monk and John Coltrane (he played on one of the iconic 'Live at the Village Vanguard' sessions), he was encouraged to start his own ensemble and champion a fusion that's still out on its own, best absorbed on sets like 1958's 'Jazz Sahara' and 'Sounds of Africa' from 1962.

Thomas, Grip, Gerbal and Wright formed [Ahmed] to celebrate Abdul-Malik's outsized but under-sung contribution to jazz, playing a raft of shows and releasing the ecstatic 'Super Majnoon' last year. But 'Giant Beauty' is an even more boundless exploration of the canon, recorded at long-running Stockholm art hot-spot Fylkingen's Festival of Other Music in 2022. On each of the event's five nights, [Ahmed] performed a different composition, stretching comparatively brief tracks like the six-minute 'African Bossa Nova' into sprawling album-length interrogations that adhere to three core rules: No discussion, no plan and no solos. [Ahmed] slim down the sonic palette on their almost 50-minute version of 'Nights on Saturn', losing Bilal Abdurrahman's haunting Korean reeds and Abdul-Malik's dextrous oud flutters and filling the gaps with fluidly evolving, energetic phrasing. Not a cover, exactly, it's described by the band as a process of "versioning", deconstructing the component elements and working out how to capture the essence without following the set path. Thomas uses his piano almost percussively, hitting the keys as if he's in communion with drummer Gerbal, who winds dizzy rolls around the dissonant crashes. And Wright wrings his alto horn into an overblown wail, mirroring the original track's non-Western arsenal without mimicking it completely.

Abdul-Malik's recording of 'Oud Blues' is a restrained slow-burner, with its walking double-bass met on the fringe with twanging, plectrum-hit oud vamps. In the hands of [Ahmed] it dissolves into a different universe; the bassline's still there to draw us in, but the quartet use this simply as a jumping-off point, lavishing it with ASMR alto smacks and frenetic hard bop piano phrases that evolve into crashing waves of militaristic drumming and swirling, dissonant horns. And there's little of the characteristic, levitational swing of the original left on [Ahmed]'s version of 'African Bossa Nova', that the band tease into an extended riot of shifting rhythms and freeform skronk that periodically turns on itself, sponging up some of Abdul-Malik's recognizable themes before wringing them out onto the ground. Recorded by John Chantler and bundled with a book featuring texts from Silvia Tarozzi, Magnus Granberg, Nate Wooley, Valerie Mol, Pär Thörn and Lars Grip and drawings from Guillaume and Aliocha Delcourt, it's a monumental package that helps affirm Abdul-Malik's rightful place in history - jazz heads, you won't wanna miss this one.

items.body:
Eminent Scottish small pipes maestro Brìghde Chaimbeul (pronounced Bree-chu Campbell) utterly commands our attention with her extraordinary, magickal follow-up to a 2023 album with big pipes player, Colin Stetson, and credits on records with Caroline Polachek and Rhodri Davies. Playing smallpipes and singing in her native Gaelic, Chaimbeul liquefies traditional standards, emphasising heaving drones, magickal chants and tactile, evocative sonic flourishes - unmissable gear for admirers of Laura Cannell, Nyahh Records, Pauline Oliveros, Harry Górski-Brown, Lankum.

Few albums ground us so physically in the sights, smells and histories of a place as 'Sunwise' does with Scotland. Chaimbeul is keenly aware of the aesthetic implications of the smallpipes - bellows-blown bagpipes that can be played over extended periods of time (and indoors, handily) - and has been refining her approach for long enough that she doesn't need to rely on overfamiliar motifs. Rather, she's able to imagine a stark, minimalist whorl of sound that outlines her themes without retreading churned-up folk festival ground. If you copped her debut 'The Reeling' or 2023's 'Carry Them With Us' then you'll have an idea of what to expect, but it's hard to express how focused 'Sunwise' is compared to its predecessors. 

Of the eight parts, three are largely original compositions placed alongside hearty renditions of old works. Brìghde comes into her own on the new parts, notably personalised in a spoken word coda by her father, Aonghas Phàdraig Chaimbeul, closing a duet with Seamus Heath’s organ on ‘Duan’ that invokes the way folklore’s collective memory is adapted down the ages, whilst her brother Eòsaph Chaimbeul joins her in the hypnotic, lilting cadence of her parting vignette, ‘The Rain Is Wine and the Stones Are Cheese’, dedicated to the darkest days of the year in a vocal style of canntaireachd, closely mimicking the bagpipes. 

Arguably the most striking parts, however, are the longer-form opening couplet of landscaping instrumental  ‘Dùsgadh/Waking’, and ‘A’ Chailleach’ where her voice almost imperceptibly harmonises with the her pipes, accompanied by Colin Stetson on sax, only to beautifully break into full song halfway. Along with the pulsating bass undulation of ‘Bog an Lohan’ and the goosepimpling plangency of her jam with a trio of uilleann pipers  ’Sguabag/The Seeper’, it’s all deeply special stuff, likely to catch you off guard with its stark beauty.

We hear enough records that claim this level of connection with the land and its history, but it's honestly rare to come across a set that truly walks the walk. The more you study 'Sunwise', the more it comes alive - a truly extraordinary achievement.

items.body:
Jazzy 1977 rework of a traditional Japanese wedding song, backed with Visible Cloaks’ weightless ambient electronic remix

The 1977 version was conceived by Jazz man Jun Arasaki and his group Nine Sheep, and executed in one take (this recording) on five sanshin, four winds, piano, bass, percussion and drums for a TV broadcast. It’s somehow solemn yet joyous in a slow and stately way, with lyrics describing how “beautiful buds unfold”.

Fourth World inhabitants and dreamers Visible Cloaks remix ‘Kajyadhi Fu Bushi’ in their own image, resulting a diaphanous, gauzy swell of harmonised synth chorales infiltrated by playful ghosts in the machine and weft with elusive traces of the original vocal to sound like a Google deep dream reverie of the real thing.

items.body:
Mercurial electro-techno steppas and rollers by LA’s Maude Vôs, moonlighting from Delusional Records onto fresh label, Gravity Pleasure.

The six tracks of ‘Medicinal Properties’ pull from Vôs’ extramusical cues of queer culture, travels in Ireland, Iceland and Montreal, and their natural worlds, for an elegantly mesmerising take on breakbeat techno modernism. Cinematic sound design and whirring rhythmic programming wraps up in calm yet urgent forms, ranging from the needlepoint step and hyaline synth pads of ‘Orr Kore’ and the EP’s title tune, thru the clipped sort of post-dubstep gait to ‘Sap Sanctuary’, and halfstep cyberdub lean of ‘Jasmine Seson’, to windswept electrostep tekkerz in ‘Endless Fliuch’, and dBridge-esque widescreen Autonomic sublime of ‘Swimming Saracnade’.

items.excerpt: Autechre's reissue engine reaches their outstanding 2008 album, featuring definitive moments of their near 40 year (and ongoing) run. ‘Quaristice’ is Rob Brown and Sean Booth’s 9th studio album as Autechre, conceived some 20 years up-to-the-hilt in their thing, and depicting the duo emerging into a sort of hybrid live x studio jam style that’s distinguished much of their work thus far. items.body:
Autechre's reissue engine reaches their outstanding 2008 album, featuring definitive moments of their near 40 year (and ongoing) run.

‘Quaristice’ is Rob Brown and Sean Booth’s 9th studio album as Autechre, conceived some 20 years up-to-the-hilt in their thing, and depicting the duo emerging into a sort of hybrid live x studio jam style that’s distinguished much of their work thus far. However archänlèy, it’s still not even the best version - that honour is reserved to the 2.5hr digital-only ‘Quaristice.Quadrange.ep.ae’ brimming with extended versions, including an hour long mix of ‘Perlance subrange 6-36’ and deadly 10’ mix of ‘Tkakanren’ - but suffice it to say we’re made up to see this one in the wild on vinyl, at least.

The follow-up to a pivotal standout, 2004’s ‘Untilted’ (also reissued this year), ‘Quaristice’ really felt like a future upgrade to the system on its release in 2008. Completely unconcerned with prevailing or emerging trends of dubstep or UKF at the time, it sees the duo follow their noses for hardware/ software jams into the proper mutant body music, milling limbs to the meanest 112BPM electro swag in the twin-rotor electro hip hop gnash of ‘Tankakern’, and utterly wrecking the senses in the blizzard dynamic of ‘Fol3’, or manipulating sinew with deviant liquid B-Boy tekkerz on ’90101-5l-l’ - each of which feature in even better versions on the 2nd disc (and frankly better yet in their alternative extensions of the digi-only version). 

There are flashes of the melodic and harmonically curious Autechre we all know and love in opener ‘Altibzz’ (their love note to the magic of Altrincham), the aerated strings of ‘Theswere’, and almost Lynchian noir of ‘Notwo’, yet the whole thing feels to trigger muscle memories and flashbacks to club physicality, as felt in the corresponding live show at Pure in Manchester at the time. The mad thing is, as judged from recent live show, they still sound as rudely uncompromising and propulsive now, 17 years later, perhaps more than ever

items.body:
Jan Jelinek and Alan Abrahams of Portable/Bodycode fame come together on perhaps the most substantial new Jelinek project in years - recalling his own classic Gramm and Farben projects with this low-lit set of simmering, frayed House burners. Really stong!

The two were on each other's radars for years, but didn't come in contact properly until Abrahams brought Jelinek to play at one of his Süd Electronic parties, where they began to mull over the idea of a collaboration. Over the years, they built up a rapport; Abrahams would fire over material that Jelinek would work into the stems, slowly building up the confidence to take more and more risks. He began to fixate on Abrahams voice, ignoring the rest of the instrumentation and threaded it through his usual lattice of concrète sounds in a sort of classic Farben mode.

Farben's a good reference point, particularly for 'Forever', the set's housey-est cut. Jelinek explains in the accompanying press release that the raw vocal had reminded him of "classic house" and that's where we start, with jazzy keys gassing up Abrahams' soulful vox. By the time we hit the halfway point, Jelinek's processes have taken over, with buzzing synths and snowballing percussion that create a dense wall of insectoid noise and interference before the track fades dramatically to silence. It's the most propulsive material Jelinek's been involved with for ages; on '87BPM', he sways Abrahams' wordless groans into a trotting, ping pong shuffle and 'All One' does a thing with tape stop melodies and drunken vocals that sound like an offcut from the CMYK series of EPs.

items.body:
Eglo co-founder & Rinse FM resident Alex Nut continues to come into his own as a producer with deep cuts of beatdown soul and broken beat sagely nodding in the direction of Dego, Waajeed, Theo Parrish.

Nut is feeling the funk three different ways on his 3rd solo EP issued in the past 12 months. His DJ-honed club instincts and feel for timeless soul feed forward into the lo-slung shimmy of ‘Bright’, glazing a Detroit-style house strut with harmonised and cut-up vocal motifs bathed in warmest keys, before lacing it with a skudgy acid line for later in the night on its ‘Re-FreQ’ mix. The heat keeps knees up, hips swivelling, on a classic Y2K West London broken beat flex mutual to his and Floating Points’ tastes, whereas ‘Duck Duck’ really dials it down to with a bed ways glyde in its velvet-clad bass and dreamily vapourised chords.

items.body:
On his compelling debut bow for Kiran Sande’s Lost Domain, multi-faceted post-techno bard Thomas Bush pushes from ambient elegy to exquisite timbral fuckery and bedsit blooz with a poetic grasp of minimalist brutalism akin The Automatics Group, Dale Cornish, Lolina, John T. Gast.

Since the ‘00s, in a multitude of pseudonyms - RAP, Citrus & Musk, cATHOLIC CHURCH - Thomas Bush has led a strange dance across styles and labels in a mode that can loosely be described as post dance music; “post” as in the forms are there, but gutted and inhabited by a more curiously reflective, experimental spirit. That taxonomy may well send some listeners fleeing signposts of indulgent whimsy, however in context of Bush’s music it signals the paradoxical dualities of his work between calm stasis and pulsing drive, or composition/deconstruction, all tied with a fine feel for consonance/dissonance that really lends the album a fascinating edge. 

Never overbearing, always reserved, the songs play out with a seductive intimacy from the solemn transition of pump organ phrasing into lapsed choirboy techno on ‘Down a Precipice’ to a real standout of brain-tickling timbral shivers delivered like a Loren Connors chamber nocturne in ‘Galvar.’ The combo of concentrated, puristic synth pulse and barely-there vox to ‘Escovitch’ also impresses, imagining something like a strung-out Dale Cornish x Theo Burt jam, and at its core the 8’ choral thrummer ‘Excommunication’ again feels to negotiate the sacred and profane with a detached gauziness that brings one uncannily close to his conception of a private rave musick, as executed with a wickedly briny tang in the tumpin’ warehouse blooz of ’Seether.’

items.body:
Class vinyl debut of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry’s live band bass player, Slim Levy, trading in charmingly dare-to-differ cosmic dub sorcery on an ideal home for this type of lark - Disrupt’s indomitable Jahtari.

Aside to private dubplates, ’Snippet Sounds’ is the French multi-instrumentalist’s first record, proper; a carousel of gently psychoactive and subtle skews on convention that chimes with soundsystema nd dub outliers such as Sheriff Lindo or Tapes, or the rest of the of the Jahtari kru, for that matter. 

Taking equal cues from his former bandleader (he played on Perry’s last tour), and The Beach Boys’ ‘Pet Sounds’, the set reels to 14 succinct and DJ-ready parts, dancing between toytronic vignettes and more fully formed knees-ups that echo the strange, innovative spectres of ‘70s Black Ark output via more lo-fi tekkerz.

To play favourites, we advise checking for the plucky, air-step skank of ‘Chalaladub’, the rickety ‘Chim Cherie’ vintage vibe of ‘Characteristics’ and ‘Train Train’, or perfectly sozzled drunken master style of ‘The Evil Cowboy Condor’, thru the early digickal bubbler ‘Wake Up John’. But ultimately we reckon it’s best taken in one go, where the tidgier bits come into their own in an album context.

items.body:
The Genioh Yamashirogumi collective, most famous for 1988's Symphonic Suite Akira, feature on this incredible 1986 album that shares much of Akira's musical DNA with expansive orchestrations performed by more than 200 musicians and taking in Tibetan horns, Bulgarian-style chorales, rhythmelodic gamelan and central African field recordings rich with hypersonic frequencies​.

Undoubtedly the most vital reissue of the year, 'Ecophony Rinne' is the precursor to 1988's iconic 'Symphonic Suite Akira' - and to our minds is even better. The sheer ambition here is remarkable, smashing together thousands of years of culture and nascent technology, collaborating with literally hundreds of musicians and figuring a blueprint for experimental music that's rarely properly examined.

We know you've heard the 'Akira' soundtrack. And we still remember catching it for the first time, wondering why its future-ancient sounds - Baleinese gamelan orchestra chimes, Japanese noh chants, baroque chorals and unsettling synthesized elements - worked so well with the sci-fi milestone's viscerally affecting post-apocalyptic themes. To Katsuhiro Otomo, the music was never an afterthought: it had been developed before the film had even been figured out; the rhythm of the action is utterly in debt to Geinoh Yamashirogumi's innovative score. And we can follow those roots directly to 'Ecophony Rinne', an album that appeared to little fanfare (in the West, at least) back in 1986. The man behind the project was Dr. Tsutomu Ōhashi, an agricultural scientist, composer and prestigious author who's better known, at least in musical circles, by his pseudonym Shoji Yamashiro. When he was at university, he studied microbiology, but he found himself drawn to music in parallel, learning Western-style conducting and working with the Hato no Kai student choir in the 1960s. And it was this experience that led him to question Western musical logic; he saw the limitations of the system, founding Geinoh Yamashirogumi in 1974 as a reaction - an opportunity to share his radically open-minded sonic philosophy with curious minds in his community.

Yamashiro avoided "classically-trained" musicians, preferring to work with amateurs who enjoyed music's instinctual qualities as much as he did - and he refused to box himself into a single culture's creative output. He didn't actively avoid the Western canon, but he didn't focus on it either, examining Indonesian folk music, Hindustani forms, Bulgarian choral music and African indigenous traditions with the same breathless energy. In fact, it was during a trip to the Democratic Republic of Congo, where he lived with the Mbuti peoples in the Ituri Rainforest, when the seeds of 'Ecophony Rinne' were sown. Yamashiro realized that the Mbuti's improvised polyphonic music, made completely without scores or schools, was just as complex as the renaissance choral music he'd studied at college. This revelation backed up the ideas that had driven him to found Geinoh Yamashirogumi in the first place and when he returned to Japan, he began to develop a suite that didn't concentrate on a single aspect of music or even pure sound itself, fixating on the harmonies that bring together millennia of evolution. This wasn't world music, it was human music that attempted to work completely outside of the usual hierarchies.

Of course, something this ambitious wouldn't work unless it was reined in masterfully, and that's where Yamashiro really excels. If you've heard 'Symphonic Suite Akira', you'll already recognize the general aesthetic, but it's the scope of 'Ecophony Rinne' that puts it in its own bracket. It's too vague to call it cinematic, even; we get a general feeling of scope from the immense, teeming soundscapes, constructed meticulously by Yamashiro from the work of literally hundreds of collaborators, field recordings he collected throughout the world and samples he'd been archiving for years, but it's because his sonic references have been used by other since the release of 'Ecophony Rinne' and 'Symphonic Suite Akira' that we hear it as such a relatable narrative. When it was released, there was simply nothing else like it - a true polyphonic experience that treats different elements like shades of color, brushing rhythmelodic Balinese gamelan sequences next to screeching birds and insects captured in the rainforest, references to Bach and Beethoven as well as Balkan folk choirs and processed kosmische synths. It's breathtaking, impossible even to absorb in a single sitting - we realize we harp on about deep listening, but occasionally a close, focused session is all that will do a record justice.

It doesn't even stop there; when Yamashiro was checking the test pressing for the album, he noticed that the vinyl version sounded much better than the digital files and wanted to know exactly why. So of course, he enlisted a team of listeners and hooked them up to medical equipment to test their brainwaves. He realized that because CDs usually had the sound rolled off at 22.05kHz, there were seemingly inaudible ultra-high frequencies being lost that were crucial to the experience - sounds that would be found naturally in verdant environments and sounds that make gamelan orchestras so undeniably rich. He dubbed this "the hypersonic effect" and established Studio Terra, a fidelity research lab, to develop special speakers to replicate the proper sound of the music. Thankfully, for anyone with a good set of speakers, this new reissue, the first proper one since its original release four decades ago, has been treated with the respect it deserves, mastered at half-speed at Abbey Road and handled with 'nuff care so that the frequencies are preserved. You might not be able to hear it, but you fully feel that there's something special happening - we'd even say that 'Ecophony Rinne' is one of the most prescient, most innovative records of the 1980s. Essential doesn't come close.

items.body:
Rattly, stripped-to-the-bone IDM gear that harks back to simpler times, BOT1500's second proper album is simple and elegant, more concerned with the emotional weight of its melodies than the complexity of its beats.

You might remember Shinichi Koboyashi's last BOT1500 album 'Surreal', that appeared back in 2022 on AD93's Lith Dolina sublabel. And since then he's been relentlessly prolific on his Bandcamp, issuing regular single track updates that chart his creative process. But 'The Black Sea' is his first longer set in a while, assembling a handful of tracks that highlight his recent interest in minimalism, emotion and dub production techniques. The familiar monosynth groans and dry, jazzy breaks on 'Abstract Springs' might resemble Squarepusher for a moment, but it's much chillier, sparser gear, with space around each element that softens the impact of the hyperactive edits. And on 'Shadows', that same mood pervades the track even when the beats have been silenced; Koboyashi gives just as much importance to his chiming analog synths, coaxing out fragile melodies that sound as if they've been plucked out of time.

And there's a precision to his programming that's immediately impressive. On 'XB 1', his soft focus glitches and woody hits graze the post-dubstep landscape but subtly reframe it, setting the meticulous rhythms against echoing single note sine hits and melancholy pads. And the track's sequel 'XB 2' is an even harder punch to the gut, with exquisite melodies and knife-edge drums that shuttle us right back to 1996 for a moment, an underground dominated by Clear Records, Spymania and Rephlex.

items.body:
Retrospective of elegant rare groove and folk-pop from Phnom Penh’s golden age of sound in the 1960s and 1970s.

"In those vibrant years, the city pulsed with music: rock bands, crooners, and traditional ensembles blended East and West, shaping a uniquely Cambodian pop that shimmered with hope and modernity. Amid this flourishing scene, So Savoeun’s voice stood out—silken yet powerful, intimate yet expansive, carrying with it the promise of a new era. This collection brings together rare and long-unheard recordings, including luminous duets with legendary contemporaries Meas Saman, Lek Savath, and Sinn Sisamouth.

Each track is more than just a song—it is a fragment of memory, a preserved echo of nights when Phnom Penh’s dance halls and radios overflowed with rhythm and possibility. In her own words, hearing these songs resurface is like opening a long-buried chest of jewels, hidden beneath the dust of history and now gleaming again after half a century. Her voice, once thought lost to time, reemerges like the cicada whose chant reverberates endlessly through the forest—an eternal call that bridges silence and remembrance. Her music is more than nostalgia; it is testament and rebirth. It continues to resonate, not only with those who lived through that golden era, but with new generations discovering its beauty for the first time. Through this release, the past breathes again—tender, luminous, and unforgettably alive."

items.body:
Vaporwave catalyst Spencer Clark (The Skaters) responds to the paintings of Belgium-based Croat artist Vedran Kopljar with some of his lushest, worm-holing, inter-dimensional synth trips.

Some 15 years since the first instalment of The Spectacle of Light Abduction, Clark takes cues from Kopljar’s vividly surrealistic windows of invention to dive headlong into polychromatic alleys of the mind. A sense of ceremonial ritual emerges in passage from the herded rhythms and aeolian winds of ‘Abyssfields’ into the high plains drift evoked by ‘Abomination Plateaus’, adapting prevailing winds of new age ambient and Troma-esque synth gunk to put a proper breeze behind one’s noumenal sails and leave lots to the imagination. Trust it’s not the corny signposted pish that vaporwave has become, but a visionary, world-building immersion in Clark’s magnificent inner world, a place familiar yet strangely displaced from normality, where the synths exhale pure DMT-like fractals and tickle atavistic reaches of the amygdala.

items.body:
Tomoyoshi Date and Stijn Hüwels's "Tatemono (建物)" via LAAPS

"Tomoyoshi Date and Stijn Hüwels met for the first time in 2015 in Tokyo, being introduced to each other by Chihei Hatakeyama. That same evening, they recorded what would later become Hochu-Ekki-Tou, their first album, released on Home Normal in 2019, followed by 遠き火、遠き雲 (A Distant Fire, A Distant Cloud) in 2021 on LAAPS.

Tomoyoshi Date creates acoustic and organic sounds with a little touch of digital processing. He began to create electronic music in 1998. In 2003, he forms the group Opitope with Chihei Hatakeyama (released by SPEKK), in 2012 the group ILLUHA with Corey Fuller (released by 12k), and the group Melodia with Federico Durand (Home Normal). His solo albums were released from Flyrec (2009, Japan) and Own Records (2011, Luxembourg). Also he worked as emergency doctor until 2014, and started his ambient oriental medical clinic "Tsuyukusa Clinic" in Tokyo since 2014. Tomoyoshi currently resides in Narita, close to Tokyo.

Stijn Hüwels has a profound fascination for minimalism. He's using mainly layers of processed guitar and field recordings. He released on Dauw, mAtter, Eilean Rec., Home Normal, White Paddy Mountain and Slowcraft/Lifelines. He released albums in collaboration with Chihei Hatakeyama, Norihito Suda, An Moku and Ian Hawgood. Together with James Murray he forms Silent Vigils. Stijn lives and works in Leuven and Brussels, Belgium. He's also curating Slaapwel Records since 2014, a label dedicated to music to fall asleep with."

items.body:
Peak Oil mooch in our back yard again with a strong album from YOUTH & Shotta Tapes alum Leo - the latest in their line of UK mutants (Paperclip Minimiser, Low End Activist, Wrecked Lightship) and a definitive statement of classic uk dub-as-method in electroid 2-step and crooked dembow forms.

A whirring cog in the Manchester machine, Leo has spent the 2020s rent in brooding negative space. His 4th album, ‘Cicada Burnt’ emerges in six segments that harness his drummer’s sleight of hand and feel for textured production on structures that teem with hi-tech sound design, insectoid detail and weathered pressure systems. No doubt it’s his most impressive artistic statement thus far, straddling key, extramusical reference points nabbed from his roots in Pennine Oldham landscapes and work strafing the industrial city downhill, and in that sense comparable with the Skam/NMB nexus or DDS’ cloud-seeding rufige.

Under the ochre artwork of Sean Clarke, who does Leo’s live visuals, the album smoulders with a dusky light and particulates in the air, conjuring immersive environmental settings and subtle tensions between the anticipatory rhythms and dread gloom. We can hear coruscating echoes of Paperclip Minimiser’s pendulous metric intricacy via Autechre in ‘Qwershape’, and his adroit percussive instincts on the tight electro-rolls of a ‘Jetti’ reminding us of Gescom's Cybotron-sampling classic 'Puzl', as well as low key Skam legend Mike Williamson - the guy behind that sick Grace Jones edit on Mask 400. His feel for syncopated nuance is zipped tightest in the grimy dembow of ‘Descant’, and likewise a weightless ‘Spirit Level (Prescript)’ demonstrating patiently poised, heightened proprioceptions, held in balance with the tendon-twitching steppas closer ‘Spirit Level’.

items.body:
Fleet-heeled, mystic industrial steppas by Naples’ finest, propelled on his private press label FFO John T. Gast, TNT Roots, Ossia, Muslimgauze, Conrad Pack

Eyes-down, knee-raising pressure for the fiends right here, from one Giovanni Napolano, aka NPLGNN. After proving his mettle in the live arena, @Razzmatazz, Barcelona, for Homemade Soundsystem in ’24, he swivels to his own steam here, meting out a bone-rattling zinger akin JTG or Element on ‘Tribes of the Present’, and swinging hard into mutant dancehall on ‘Lullaby Dint ‘O Scur (Battente I)’, and its siren-sounding ‘Battente II’ version. Harder yet, ‘Rruin (_Ashbah Steppa)’ cracks out the choral pads and turbo depth-charged subs on a Conrad Pack tip, and ‘Alba Del Domani (No Fall)’ hits Nkisi-esque levels of tekno doom hoof.

items.body:
Revisiting their debut album '.After', Tujiko Noriko and Adrian Corker commission a suite of remixes, bringing in Koshiro Hino ov YPY, goat (JP) and KAKUHAN fame, Tashi Wada, DJ Trystero, Shojiro Nakaoka and DJ ojo to put their spin on the source material.

The original album only took Noriko and Corker a couple of days in the studio, but they wired the results to percussionist and arranger George Barton, who took it to the next level. They continue the thought on '.After Again', dishing out the stems to a carefully pruned list of collaborators - artists whose distinctive sounds only extend the original album's sonic universe. And of course it's the YPY version of the album's opening track 'Yasashii Sayonora' that'll have most of y'all chomping at the bit; Hino turns Corker and Noriko's source material to dust, time-stretching Noriko's vocal and zeroing in on the stuttering percussion and rusted turntable loops. Adding his signature jerks, he fills the track with clattering metallic clangs, twisting the voices into downsampled groans from a neighboring cyber-reality.

Tokyo's DJ Trystero opts for a different but similarly unique approach on his two reworks, the "All Frills" remix of 'Toku No Minato' and his "Naive Declension" version of the same track. On the former, he isolates almost indistinguishable elements of the original, setting the ghost traces to a typically deep, dubby groove and on the latter, creates a rugged, gear-heavy jam from the remains. It's actually Nakaoka who provides the weirdest - yet strangely most recognisable - versions, using his custom generative code to match Noriko's voice with whirring interference and warbling digital detritus.

items.body:
War.Poem by Chris Connelly, via Dirter Promotions.

“ "WAR.POEM” was recorded at THE ROCK NOIR studio in 2025/2026 as a reaction to a piece I read on the Israeli military use of FLECHETTE SHELLS in Gaza, this led to a much deeper study of the 20th/21st century history of war. The album was composed entirely using a TAPE O MATIC 710 reel to reel from 1958, a 1960’s mayfaair JVC reel to reel, aa 1965 G.E. solid state portable reel to reel from 1965, a portable 1970’s Panasonic cassette player, a ring modulator as well as various other effects and synths.

The loop that is the basis for WAR POEM ZERO which takes up the whole of side one, happened by accident when I put a reel on the wrong way up, it produced aa sound of such great melancholy and beauty, I just let it play…

This album owes a debt to “SWANSONG” by NURSE WITH WOUND from the album “A MISSING SENSE” where experimental sound is used as an anti war protest.

- Chris Connelly 2026"

You are unlikely to hear a record of such brutal intensity, or indeed authenticity as this. To call it “old school industrial” would be to do it a disservice, but also not THAT wide of the mark. It is packaged sympathetically to Chris’ previous release for the label, the long sold out LP “White Phosphorous”."

items.body:
Elijah Minnelli and co.’s skewed rap trio, Damos Room, proceed from five years of dare-to-differ self-releases with a moody, club-edged EP for the ace All Centre label, bolstered by remixes from Pauline, James Massiah, Dome Zero and Horse Militia

On ‘Volcano’ Minnelli touches the mic in style far-removed from his weirdo cumbia dub charms, rolling in an accented UKHH style over dub skewed dancehall production recalling vintage Roots Manuva and New Flesh For Old in the OG and extended mixes. 

The remixes tilt ‘Volcano’ to the edge of the ‘floor, with Pauline resetting it to a trippy sort of digi-cumbia slosh and Dome Zero’s Canned Laughter Mix emphasising a sort of rugged Bristol industrial lean. James Massiah wholly replaces the vocal with his own, on re-tuned electro-dancehall ballast, and disco-pointed edit with Horse Militia.

items.body:
Originally released in 1995, Rachel Goswell and Neil Halstead's Mojave 3 debut 'Ask Me Tomorrow' has finally been given the deluxe treatment - remastered by Abbey Road and back in print for the first time in years. 

It's hard to believe that 'Ask Me Tomorrow' appeared less than a year after 'Pygmalion'. Slowdive's last album flopped at the time, though - their fusion of waved electronica and shoegaze wouldn't really catch on until a few decades later, long after the band had splintered. And in their wake, Halstead and Goswell traded the sounds of deep space for something more earthy, drawing on their love of Bob Dylan and Townes Van Zandt to record a demo of country-tinged acoustic pop. The tape made its way to 4AD's Ivo Watts-Russell, and was quickly bumped up into a full album that's probably the band's most consistently enjoyable. 

Goswell and Halstead sound refreshingly comfortably making echoing, Lynchian alt-country - something that shouldn't be too surprising to anyone who obsessed over the windy, whimsical 'Pygmalion' fave 'Blue Eyed An' Clear'. And they're still trapped in the shadow of shoegaze past on their debut, obscuring their vocals with reverb and slowing their songs down to a sensual crawl. Opener 'Love Songs on the Radio' lies between Slowdive and Mazzy Star and Goswell has rarely sounded better, while Halstead sounds almost like Nick Drake on the charming 'You're Beautiful'. The best is saved for last: 'Mercy', the album's dark, melancholy finale that sounds as if it's waving goodbye to an era that's already disappeared.

items.body:
Lechuga Zafiro, Low Jack, OSSX and Sylvere turn in a suite of remixes for last year's 'Burbujas', Daniel Pineda's first solo EP in almost a decade.

Capturing the essence of Einhundert's legendary parties as well as extending the impact of Pineda's EP, 'Burbujas (Remixes)' quite intentionally surveys the underground club landscape and joins up its landmarks. Paris-based beatmaker Sylvere is up first and pays respect to his roots in the Caribbean with a bouyon version of 'Motif Mambo', switching up its rhythm and interjecting with energetic drops. Then Low Jack weighs in with his twanging version of Pineda's "baby rave" banger 'Siq One' adding a gruesome distorted bassline and chest-crushing gated kicks. Jersey duo (and Einhundert regulars) OSSX drive 'Invocations' through the East Coast with a pneumatic kick-break thrust that's neatly spruced up with vocal slices and rave-ready organ vamps and it's down to the always reliable Lechuga Zafiro to tie a bow around the whole set with an expectedly inventive tribute to DJ Rolando.

2026 has been light on the club highlights, but this one hits the spot.

items.body:
Essential listening FFO Time Is Away, Jon Collin or the 'Bagpuss' soundtrack, Rory Salter, aka Malvern Brume, confronts cutesy British folk nostalgia on 'For Red Riverbank', using 'The Wind in the Willows' references, sobering newsreel snippets and straight-to-tape acoustic jams to develop a faded image of labour inequality.

Nostalgia is supposed to be digestible - a cultural banana that gives the mind all familiarity without friction. But munch on the same gear for too long and it starts to cause irritation; it's hard not to notice, for example, that the prim Ghost Box-style Gen Z hauntology has reached its logical conclusion. Whatever it was saying about the UK's welfare-era lost futures has not only been photocopied half to death, but it's also been added to the slop machine, spat out as empty "content" that's almost hypnotically nauseating - especially when you consider the state of welfare in 2026. Thankfully, we're not the only people to have noticed; Salter takes aim at the romance of British folk culture on his proper The Sprigs debut, using a framework we'll all be familiar with - Kenneth Grahame's Edwardian children's classic 'The Wind in the Willows'. It's important to note that the book was already steeped in nostalgia when it was first published back in 1908, a reflection on nature in the face of mass industrialization, as the affordable Ford Model T was beginning to appear on roads for the first time. So it's a more complex reference than you might initially figure, and Salter uses this backdrop to root his investigation of British labour history and the very meaning of tradition.

We've all heard remnants of folk music vibrate through the collective consciousness over the years, not least in the wake of the New Weird America movement of the early '00s. And Salter's awareness of these sounds and the perpetual churn that followed is crucial; he doesn't subvert them as such, but repurposes them, hitting on themes and sequences that connect us to the country's soil and textures that help to rub away some of nostalgia's entrancing sparkle. The 12-minute opener 'come along, back home' sounds at first like an old protestant hymn being bellowed through broken pipes and Salter keeps scraping away at history, collaging textured environmental loops with simplistic, almost naive folk songs, peculiar resonances and, occasionally, what sounds like an old recorder. And it's the back-and-forth between gravelly noise and nostalgic naivety that makes 'For Red Riverbank' so inviting. The short, sharp 'Ratty & the moles get to work' is just as jolly as its title, sounding as brittle and evocative as Sandra Kerr and John Faulkner's fluttered folk songs that lifted Oliver Postgate's 'Bagpuss'.

And Salter doesn't just look back through rose-tinted spectacles, he juxtaposes these evocative sounds with sobering recordings of newsreaders, politicians and union leaders, who complete a quite genuine picture of the recent past. Like George Eliot's Middlemarch, that imagined a fictional Midlands town four decades prior to its writing, the inviting idealized setting was a Trojan horse for Eliot's real theme: the 1832 Reform Act that upended the electoral system. Salter employs the same sleight of hand, introducing us to a world we know and love before drip, drip, dripping the politics we so desperately need.

items.body:
Perhaps the most interesting PAN in a minute; ‘Lila’ is the label debut from Paris-based Algerian Mohamed Bourouissa, best known as a visual artist but now offering a glimpse into his musical practice for the first time, blending highly unusual ambient pulses with autotuned, low-lit vocals, recorded on the fly using a keyboard, mixer, microphone and effects. It runs like some lost 1980’s private press, tipped FFO early Yves Tumor, Yungwebster, Space Afrika, AYYA, Future, Kareem Lotfy.

Bourouissa’s first solo album finds the 48 year old artist capturing the permeable membrane between Paris' various communities through a dream diary of hazed ambient reflections, cloud rap inversions and bass-heavy club malfunctions. It follows his work over decades incorporating music as a phantom thread of his practice in photography, sculpture, and video, and perfectly conveys a sense of longing and melancholy central to Arabic classical and pop songs mediated via an electronic hypermodernism . The album is an intimate, sometimes unsettling experience, aptly described as “hypnagogic” by PAN, as heard in its tendency to dreamlike slowness and the layered haze of FX and xenharmonic chords that shroud and wreath his melismatic woes. 

The dozen tracks play out through autotuned vocal plumes familiar from work by Ayshay, Rainy Miller or Future, crossed with the type of deep blooz oozing from that superb Taymour x Bareetlblad turn on the diy label earlier this year. Each track taps a different pole into the album's landscape, one beatless, and one filled with machinegun toms and explosive snares. The beatless tracks are peculiarly stirring and the heavier, noisier moments somehow vanish into the same aether. Bourouissa peppers the album with wild twists and turns, hitting a dark alley on the anxiety-inducing 'NMB' and descending corrugated steps to a members-only basement on 'MN'. The relief comes with the title track, a collaboration with Fanigliulo (aka Mushy) that's a tender, hopeful moment -  a clouded love song that injects some hope into the darkness.

items.body:
Special edition of Sun Ra’s classic ‘Lanquidity’, for the 25th anniversary of the label. If yr looking for a way to penetrate Ra's intimidating catalog, "Lanquidity" is a precious wormhole that gives a taste of the jazz pioneer's astral weirdness without letting it overwhelm. Transformative shit, really.

Released in a tiny edition back in 1978, "Lanquidity" is Sun Ra's attempt at cultural reconciliation. It's the ultimate flex, finding the Arkestra alien absorbing contemporary pop elements (disco, funk, soul) into his canon, before spitting them out as further cosmic strings in his pan-universal bow. The playability of "Lanquidity" has given it legs: before its reissue in 2000, the album had hardly been heard, but was spoken about in hushed tones. A couple of decades later, it's an established classic, putting Sun Ra's talent into full view and quieting some of the sprawling galaxy-brain oddness that alienates some listeners.

Recorded by Philly Jazz boss Tom Buchler (who penned enlightening liner notes about the recording experience), "Lanquidity" has Sun Ra fronting a band of over fourteen players, including Marshall Allen on alto sax and John Gilmore on tenor. Intriguingly, he also ropes in not one but two guitarists, giving the album its "Bitches Brew"-adjacent fusion fuzz, but it's the overdubbing of disembodied voices and layers of Arp and Minimoog that puts these tracks into a category all of their own. The mood Sun Ra creates is truly planetary (just flick to the album's terrifyingly tripped 'There Are Other Worlds (They Have Not Told You Of)' for proof) and while he certainly makes concessions with his stylistic choices, the pop shell is merely a Trojan horse for his vanguard forms.

Classic.

items.body:
There's a scene near the end of  Uncut Gems  where the hapless protagonist Howard Ratner, locked behind the security glass of his own shop, watches a parlay come in leg by leg. As each result lands, the magnitude of the one that follows swells, a runaway train of buzz and anxious sweats. Watching Short Span for the past 18 months has felt a lot like standing behind that glass. (Without giving away spoilers, don't worry, that's where the Ratner comparisons end.)

The Sheffield label, run by Matthew Kent—formerly of 2010s-defining mix series  Blowing Up The Workshop —has yet to lose a bet. From Yu Su's  Foundry  to  K Wata 's  Give U Space , each record raises what's staked on the next.  Uuuuuuuu  from Aarhus producer Picture, AKA Natal Zaks is the latest leg to come in—and it's a delight.
 
On the surface, it might seem like an unlikely match. To this day, Zaks is perhaps better known as  Central , who released slinky, midtempo house music as part of Regelbau (he also gave Erika de Casier her  first credit  back in 2017). Short Span, meanwhile, started out a dub techno label two years ago with notable, genre-bending early releases from Sa Pa and Mammo teeing up a widening of the roster in 2026 with the likes of Mr YT and Bot1500. You might consider the label's releases as having little in common musically—instead, the throughline is a disposition rather than a sound. Yu Su  described  Kent as having "all this in-betweenness going on," never settling into one style; Kent has put it similarly himself,  musing  that the label is "for a certain kind of identity that crosses boundaries."

Zaks, then, makes a perfect fit. There's always been something unresolved about his sound, and the traces are audible if you dig: take " Lost Touch ," from 2022's  Up And Down , a twitchy dub techno number built around a wavering synth and a sense of space you'll recognise from the Picture records. 

 Uuuuuuuu  is Zaks' second Short Span record this year, following February's  Eeeeeeee , and harder than the first. "Peeeeeee" (no relation to it's bodily namesake, seemingly) is a claustrophobic techno number with a swinging bassline and an undercurrent of unease like a wonkier Chain Reaction cut. It's reminiscent of being inside a printing factory: the looping synth line is the chug of the machinery, the filter sweep and textures like flying debris, ramping up in the closing minutes, twisting the dial even further on a sense of anxiety. Similarly, "Wooooooo" conjures up the darkest corners of the club. Carrying the air of a closing set on a German mountainside—a rave reshape of Caspar David Friedrich's quintessential painting  Wanderer above the Sea of Fog —wind sweeping around you until a hardgroove bassline introduces an element of steeliness, the summit re-cast in girders and concrete. 

There's also plenty of dubbier, womb-like moments to offset the twitchy mood. Take "Miiiiiii": the pads hold steady but never stop shifting, and beneath them sits what sounds like a springtime field recording, birds chirping into a soft kick drum. "Ziiiiiiiii" has a lighter touch still, like the lovechild of a SnPLO and Dettinger record left out to gather dust—the cycle home from a long night, the melody a hazy sun coming up, the percussion your own worn-out legs chugging you back. "Leeeeee" bridges the two worlds, and gets closer to traditional dub techno than anything else here:  Shinichi Atobe 's warmth over the pure dub glimmer of Vainqueur.

On the dub techno continuum, Picture sits closer to  Convextion  than to most of the '90s set, in both spirit and sound. Whereas Convextion once described his own music as "emotional punishment," on  Uuuuuuuu , I'd suggest Picture hits emotional levity. The material is heavy and the arrangements are crowded, yet the swing keeps everything off the floor: unquantised, the same weight stops pressing down and starts lifting. It's been on  our minds  lately that the 2020s might lack a sound of their own, that the decade has spent itself revisiting other people's halcyon days. Zaks' restless take on dub techno is proof there's still evolution inside the framework, and thrilling stuff still lies ahead.

items.artist: Fermín Suárez, Shantala Ferreyra, Gonzalo Goicoechea
items.excerpt: Las Instancias comprises Shantala Ferreyra on clarinet, Fermín Suárez on double bass, and Gonzalo Goicoechea on drums. Ferreyra is an Argentinian clarinettist and composer who graduated from the Jazz Performance Program at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory in 2024. In 2025, she released her debut album featuring her original compositions performed by her quintet, and in 2026, she was awarded a scholarship to study composition in Basel, Switzerland. Her work combines composition and improvisation.
items.body: Las Instancias comprises Shantala Ferreyra on clarinet, Fermín Suárez on double bass, and Gonzalo Goicoechea on drums. Ferreyra is an Argentinian clarinettist and composer who graduated from the Jazz Performance Program at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory in 2024. In 2025, she released her debut album featuring her original compositions performed by her quintet, and in 2026, she was awarded a scholarship to study composition in Basel, Switzerland. Her work combines composition and improvisation. Suárez is a double bass player, improviser, songwriter, and composer from Rosario, Argentina. His artistic work encompasses a wide range of genres, including jazz, tango, Argentine folk, improvised music, and classical, often mixing, stretching, and breaking the limits between languages and traditions. He co-created the punk-tango and avant-garde ensemble ‘La Rompiente’ for which he composes and arranges. In 2026, he started the solo project ‘Ola de sótano’, a double bass and vocals set with electronics, featuring songs, improvisations and spoken word. He’s also a frequent collaborator of composer and pianist Rocío Giménez López. Goicoechea is a drummer and educator specializing in jazz. He began his studies at the Leopoldo Marechal School of Arts and later continued at the Manuel de Falla Conservatory. Since 2021, he has performed with a variety of jazz-oriented ensembles. After a year devoted to live performance and composition, Las Instancias is released by the Argentine label 625 Discos, and captures the result of their ongoing collaboration so far. With no harmonic instrument, the trio leans into timbre, register, and the register distances between clarinet, bass, and drums. The pared-back format serves as the foundation upon which the group builds its identity and scribes its musical language. The ensemble work their way through various compositions (mostly written by Ferreyra and Suárez) that constantly flirt with the edges of jazz and improvised music, exploring their aesthetic possibilities and different orchestration combinations. Recorded during a session in Rosario, the album seeks to become a living reflection of a live performance, with all its nuances and dynamism. There are fierce solos rooted in jazz language contrasted with moments of introspection expressed through a more abstract idiom, all while maintaining a strong sense of tension and attention. There is a sense of a group whose members perform in proximity, without separation or post-production tricks. The recording is an intimate encounter between both the musicians and the listener. The absence of a harmonic instrument becomes a presence: a framework that pushes them toward inventive orchestration, elastic structures, and an exploration of musical language. This album contains some standout solos and ensemble work. There is a subliminal quality to this trio that makes the music fun, as well as profoundly interesting to listen to. Don’t be fooled by the opening bars of the first track. ‘Lampara Nueva’ starts like a traditional jazz piece, but develops into something extraordinary, the dialogue flowing between the clarinet, bass and percussion like water, flowing back and forth, with a swing here, a change there, and something just for the heck of it anywhere you might care to drop in. There is a taste of traditional jazz, particularly in the drum solos that emerge from the ensemble work, particularly in the second half of the number, but there is also much free playing. ‘Mucho Agora Mismo’ starts with a gentle bass solo and works itself into a frenzy, the clarinet delivering fiery solos across the percussion, with many variations in between. This is a track of many parts, blended seamlessly together. Just beautiful. ‘Dos Veces Agosto’ is a track of harmonies, rhythms, and counter-rhythms, with some bass solos, clarinet that works around the theme, and explores many musical avenues, while maintaining a connection with the central theme. ‘En Meyo’ is a clarinet solo track, with Ferreyra meditating on a theme, while ‘Ok/Off’ is a track where all three instruments lock into the same rhythmic pattern, creating a hypnotic dynamic. A bowed bass emerges, warm and resonant, before the trio returns to their lively, idea‑trading interplay. ‘Pegao’ is introduced by a bowed bass solo, over which the clarinet drops, adding light touches and a rapid change of texture, which the drums enhance, adding their own feel and colour. It is worth listening to this for the changes and rhythmic patterns that evolve, disappear, and re-emerge, led largely by the bass, whose voice is central to this number. The album closes with a second take of 'Mucho agora mismo' which is extravagant and allows each musician to deliver improvised music of the highest calibre. Las Instancias are three musicians whose shared curiosity has shaped a sound that feels both stripped back and richly alive. There’s a cohesion that makes the music both fun and deeply absorbing. You hear three musicians who trust each other enough to take risks — to push, to pull, to leave space, to fill it, to let the music breathe and then ignite. It’s intimate, inventive, and full of personality. Las instancias by Las instancias Get it on vinyl here: https://elasticstage.com/625discos/releases/las-instancias-album Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: Temperphantom, 2026 Personnel - Victor Vieira-Branco: vibraphone; Sam Yulsman: piano; John Moran: double bass; Joey Sullivan: drums. Playing the vibraphone with a relentless sense of urgency and intent while displaying a strong, distinctive compositional identity, Victor Vieira-Branco is a name to reckon with in contemporary jazz. Rooted in Philadelphia, Bark Culture is Vieira-Branco’s creative brainchild, where intriguing sonic forces feel at once dark and lyrical, sometimes effusive yet always fresh and compelling. For this date, the core trio—with John Moran on double bass and Joey Sullivan on drums—is expanded into a harmonically richer quartet with the addition of pianist Sam Yulsman. The Giant is Awkward , Bark Culture’s sophomore record, opens with “ Palace ”, whose lush theme, rhythmically vivid drive, and hip arrangement command our attention from the very first minute. The bandleader’s rolling liquidity blends seamlessly with sweeping keyboard gestures and the vibrant tangle woven by bass and drums. Sullivan does an intricate, actively propulsive job throughout, fueled by alternative-rock stamina and responsive fills. Yulsman’s “ Farce ”, the only piece not written by Vieira-Branco, is kinetic, asymmetric, and daring in its construction, pervaded by a thrilling sense of uncertainty and a fair dose of arcane postmodern psychedelia. “ Willow ” holds a powerful and consistently engaging backbone that is unafraid of odd meters and metric modulation. Impeccably framed by Yulsman’s off-kilter piano (which sounds great despite being slightly out of tune) and Vieira-Branco’s hallucinogenic vibraphone, the piece climaxes into an unpredictable, stratospheric concentration of sound. On a different register, “ Panic ” gives silence an important role, developing with a balladic feel that favors spacious atmospheres. The album closes with “ Spectrum ”, where the beauty of the instrumentation creates ebbs and flows through intricate accentuation that feels simultaneously startling and exhilarating. There’s space for drum talk before the tension mounts through authoritative bowed bass, nebulous vibraphone streams, dreamy piano sequences, and jittery drumming. With each member focused on injecting energy and emotion, Bark Culture pushes the envelope, reinventing itself as an experimental group that strikes a perfect balance between written material and open improvisation. Vieira-Branco steps forward impressively on The Giant Is Awkward , and it’s remarkable to think these pieces were recorded at the last minute while still in sketch form. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Palace ► 02 - Farce ► 03 - Willow

items.body:
The race to crown Singapore's next Malay music star is officially on. Anugerah 2026 has unveiled its Top 14 finalists, with the long-running talent competition set to premiere 25 August. The series will air live every Tuesday at 8:30 PM on Suria, mewatch, and Mediacorp Entertainment on YouTube.

Hosted by Fadli Kamsani of Mediacorp RIA 897 and actress Lydia Asyiqin, this year's finalists earned their spots after surviving The Cut — the competition's decisive final audition round. Selected from a pool of 40 hopefuls, the Top 14 impressed judges with their vocal ability, stage presence, and star potential in one of the most competitive stages of the series.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mediacorp Untukmu (@mediacorp.untukmu)

The finalists come from diverse backgrounds, ranging from students and educators to engineers, entertainers, music teachers, and content creators. Among them are former competition alumni, experienced performers, self-taught vocalists, and rising artistes looking to make their breakthrough on national television. Notable contestants include former K-Pop World Festival Best Vocalist Akif Halqi, singer-songwriter Izzan Adlan, actor Alfan Ryan, and Chariska Diva Anugrah, daughter of Anugerah 2003 champion Eka Mairina. The competition's youngest finalist is 17-year-old Darwish Sofyan, while several contestants are making their television competition debut.

The Top 14 finalists are:

Akif Halqi

Alfan Ryan

BANIE

Chariska Diva Anugrah

Darwish Sofyan

Falisha Mustafa

Farras Qushayyi

Firdaus Senin

Hirza Haizal

Izzan Adlan

Nada Fitri

Nadhrah Roslan

Syafiqah Aziz

Tahniah Shahar

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mediacorp Untukmu (@mediacorp.untukmu)

Before stepping onto the live stage, the finalists underwent a series of masterclasses led by industry veterans including Najip Ali, vocal coach Babes Conde, singer Hady Mirza, content creator Zhin Sadali, and Sujadi Siswo. The sessions covered vocal performance, stagecraft, competition strategy, media literacy, social media presence, and personal branding, preparing contestants for the demands of the competition.

Fans can also get a closer look at the contestants through Anugerah: The Cut, a five-part digital-exclusive series that goes behind the scenes of the final audition process and documents the moments that shaped this year's final lineup.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Mediacorp Untukmu (@mediacorp.untukmu)

Viewers will play an active role throughout the competition, with audience votes contributing 20% of each contestant's overall score, while the judges account for the remaining 80%. Voting opens every Wednesday during the live shows, with registered meconnect users able to cast up to 20 votes per day via Mediacorp's voting platform.

The eventual champion will take home the Anugerah 2026 title and a grand prize of $25,000, while the first runner-up will receive $10,000, sponsored by PropNex. A PropNex Special Award worth $5,000 will also be presented to one finalist.

items.body:
Artificial intelligence is no longer just reshaping how music is created — it's also proving to be a lucrative business.

A new study by Kapwing has found that the world's biggest AI music artists have generated an estimated US$6.1 million from more than 2.3 billion combined Spotify streams and YouTube views, underscoring just how quickly AI-generated music is finding mainstream audiences.

The report arrives as streaming platforms continue stepping up efforts to tackle AI-generated content. Spotify has removed millions of AI-generated and spam tracks, while Deezer recently revealed that AI-made songs now account for more than half of all new daily uploads. Despite these measures, the study suggests AI musicians continue to attract millions of listeners and viewers across major platforms.

On Spotify, the top 10 AI artists have collectively earned an estimated US$2.38 million from roughly 595 million streams. Leading the pack is Enlly Blue, a "1950s-style" AI vocalist whose catalogue has amassed 95.2 million streams, translating to an estimated US$380,800 in Spotify earnings.

YouTube paints an even bigger picture. The platform's top 10 AI music creators have generated an estimated US$3.70 million from approximately 1.75 billion views, with Cherry 葵 Nightcore accounting for more than half that figure. The creator has accumulated 941 million views, resulting in estimated earnings of nearly US$2 million.

Beyond revenue, the report highlights the scale of AI artists' reach across streaming services. Masters of Prophecy tops the overall follower rankings with 36.1 million followers across platforms, while King Willonius leads all AI musicians with 500 chart entries. Producer Don Bnnr, meanwhile, boasts the largest playlist reach, appearing on 1,852 playlists with a combined follower count of 46.7 million listeners.

Kapwing compiled the rankings using data from AiMCharts and Songstats, analysing lifetime Spotify streams, YouTube views, followers, playlist placements and chart entries. Estimated Spotify earnings were calculated using an industry-average payout of US$0.004 per stream, while YouTube estimates were based on SocialBlade's default RPM midpoint of US$2.12 per 1,000 views.

As streaming services continue introducing tools to identify and label AI-generated music, the findings suggest that some AI artists have already crossed into the mainstream, building audiences in the tens of millions and generating meaningful revenue despite increasing scrutiny.

items.body:
Singapore's BLACK ROSE, it's finally happening, The Rose are officially bringing their ROSETOPIA Asia Tour 2026 to the Lion City! The Korean alt-rock outfit will perform at The Star Theatre on 27 October, marking their long-awaited Singapore debut after years of building a devoted global following.

Presented by CK Star Entertainment, the upcoming show will see the four-piece perform fan favourites alongside songs from their upcoming album, giving Singaporean fans their first chance to experience the band's acclaimed live show in person.

Comprised of Woosung, Dojoon, Taegyeom, and Hajoon, The Rose have steadily established themselves as one of Korea's standout live acts with their heartfelt blend of alternative pop, indie rock, and emotionally driven songwriting. Since debuting with 'Sorry', the band has amassed a passionate international fanbase known as BLACK ROSE and more than 1.2 million monthly listeners on Spotify.

Their rise has only accelerated in recent years. DUAL debuted at No. 83 on the Billboard 200, while pre-release single 'Back To Me' has surpassed 92 million streams on Spotify. The band has also become a festival favourite, appearing at Lollapalooza across multiple countries before making history as the first Korean band to perform on Coachella's Outdoor Theatre stage in 2024.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CK Star Entertainment SG 🇸🇬 (@ckstar.sg)

Now, ROSETOPIA invites BLACK ROSE into a world celebrating the band's nine-year journey through music and live performance. For Singapore fans, the concert marks a milestone that has been years in the making.

items.body:
PUMA has teamed up once again with ROSÉ to introduce a graceful new addition to its iconic Speedcat family. The new Speedcat Etoile reimagines the classic motorsport-inspired sneaker with delicate satin-inspired details and a balletcore aesthetic.

The latest silhouette arrives in a soft pastel pink colourway, blending the Speedcat's signature low-profile shape with suede overlays, subtle sheen finishes, tonal branding, and ribbon laces designed to be tied into bows. The result is a feminine take on one of PUMA's most recognisable sneakers, reflecting the continued popularity of ballet-inspired fashion.

Fronted by global K-pop star ROSÉ, the campaign leans into themes of nostalgia and self-expression. The accompanying visuals place the BLACKPINK member among childhood keepsakes and personal mementos, presenting the Speedcat Etoile as a symbol of growth while celebrating individuality and confidence. The campaign's pastel palette represents "every version of you, from where you started to where you're going."

The release also marks another chapter in the resurgence of the Speedcat franchise. Since its return in 2024, the silhouette has evolved through refreshed colourways and new interpretations including the Speedcat Ballet, Speedcat Wedge, Speedcat Mule, and several limited-edition collaborations, helping cement its place as a contemporary streetwear staple.

The Speedcat Etoile will be available from 31 July via PUMA Singapore's online store and selected PUMA retailers.

items.body:
ENHYPEN and HYBE's original story franchise DARK MOON made their first-ever appearance at San Diego Comic-Con, bringing the group's vampire-inspired universe to one of the world's biggest pop culture conventions through panels, fan events, exclusive merchandise, and immersive experiences.

Held from 23 to 26 July, DARK MOON transformed parts of the San Diego Convention Center into an extension of its fantasy universe, marking a significant step in the franchise's global expansion beyond webcomics and music.

One of the weekend's biggest highlights was Bite Me: Calling All Vampires on 23 July, a panel that explored the enduring appeal of vampire stories across generations. Hosted by TV Guide Magazine's Damian Holbrook, the discussion brought together ENHYPEN, Twilight director Catherine Hardwicke, and actors Peter Facinelli and Ashley Greene. The panel examined themes of identity, belonging, and community, with ENHYPEN sharing how those ideas are reflected in DARK MOON's centuries-spanning narrative.

Elsewhere at Comic-Con, the official DARK MOON booth drew large crowds throughout the convention, with limited-edition merchandise selling out early. On 24 July, ENHYPEN also stopped by for a fan meet-and-greet, which ranked among Comic-Con's top 10 most-requested exclusives this year out of more than 150 sessions.

The celebrations continued off-site with DARK MOON BLOOD NIGHT with ENHYPEN at San Diego's House of Blues. Fans dressed in vampire-inspired outfits stepped into the world of DARK MOON through cinematic recreations of key scenes, themed performances, and specially curated food and drinks before ENHYPEN closed the evening with a talk session and live performance inspired by the franchise's story universe.

"Through the story of vampires who exist between humanity and monstrosity, DARK MOON explores the search for identity and belonging that people experience today," said Taeho Park, Head of HYBE NEXT ENTERTAINMENT BUSINESS (NEB). "At this year's Comic-Con, we demonstrated that DARK MOON is a unique transmedia IP where storytelling, music, and fan experiences reinforce one another."

The Comic-Con debut marks another milestone for HYBE's expanding transmedia ambitions, as DARK MOON continues to evolve from its webcomic origins into a franchise spanning music, live experiences, merchandise, and fan engagement alongside ENHYPEN.

items.body:
You Yokoyama is back with the next chapter of his solo journey. The SUPER EIGHT member has officially released his sophomore solo album, ROCK FOR YOU, now available to stream worldwide.

Serving as the follow-up to 2025's ROCK TO YOU, the new record marks the evolution of Yokoyama's solo project, which began as what he described as a year-long journey of growth and self-discovery. Earlier this year, the singer hinted at what was to come with a simple message to fans: "I have more to say."

The album arrives after the release of double digital singles 'Pistol' and 'KANJOU MAIGO' in April, as well as sold-out performances at Osaka Castle Hall and Zepp Haneda. Alongside those tracks, ROCK FOR YOU also includes 'Arigato', which Yokoyama debuted live in May, plus six brand-new songs featuring lyrics written by the artist himself.

One of the album's highlights is 'Pudding', a collaboration with fellow SUPER EIGHT member Shota Yasuda, who composed the music for the track. The pair previously worked together on 'cHocolate' and 'Kicyu' from Yokoyama's debut solo album, ROCK TO YOU.

Across the record, Yokoyama continues to channel his personal experiences into heartfelt rock songs, embracing vulnerability while reflecting on the challenges and growth that have shaped both his career and relationship with fans.

Following the album's release, Yokoyama will hit the road for his ROCK FOR YOU LIVE TOUR, beginning 18 August with a 12-city run across Japan.
