items.body: Moola‘s self-titled debut emerges from a meeting of seemingly distant musical worlds that reveal themselves to be remarkably compatible. Rather than a vehicle for cultural trnslation, the duo of Renata Frana and Antonella Bianco approach sound as a space of encounter shaped by listening and intuition. The album opens with “marut”, where a steady percussive pulse and gentle electronics gradually make room for the dilruba, the bowed North Indian instrument that serves as one of the record’s defining voices. “Forgotten Ritual” begins with field recordings and initially appears to inhabit a recognisably Indian sonic landscape, while “Bridge” drifts furthest into abstraction, unfolding as a dense drone piece where otherworldly electronic textures emerge and dissolve within its shifting interior. Later, “Awakening in Calcutta” is anchored by an alluring guitar refrain, and with “Uncover” field recordings return, bringing the album full circle. Throughout, percussion provides the guiding force, while the dilruba punctuates the music with a voice that is at once lyrical and restrained. Yet what makes Moola intriguing is its refusal of easy exoticism or ethnographic certainty. The titles may hint at specific places, traditions, or histories, but the music consistently evades literal geographies. These are sonic suggestions rather than destinations; imaginings instead of documentary representations. Moola reject virtuosity and grandiose gestures. Every musical action carries weight, existing in relation to what surrounds it and capable of generating further connections. The use of toys, electronics, field recordings, guitar, and dilruba never feels decorative or driven by a desire for authenticity. There is no philological impulse here, only a deep respect for traditions combined with a willingness to let sounds circulate freely between contexts. The result is an album rooted in deep listening rather than in any single musical lineage. Like the Sanskrit word mūla from which the duo takes its name — meaning “root” — these pieces feel like the beginning of a process. Beneath the surface, connections are already spreading in multiple directions, quietly preparing for whatever may emerge next. Through an email exchange, Renata Frana and Antonella Bianco gave us their own take on the production process for the album. Antonella Bianco and Renata Frana – photo by Francesca Suriano Moola feels rooted in deep listening and cultural encounter rather than in any single musical tradition. Tracks such as “Marut”, “Awakening in Calcutta” and “Scisciu” seem to evoke different geographies and histories without ever becoming straightforward ethnographic references. How do you navigate the line between inspiration, memory and imagination when drawing on sounds, places and traditions beyond your immediate experience? Honestly, we don’t think about it too much while we’re working. For us, each piece is a room, a space that we build, and then we listen to what wants to inhabit it. Of course, the places we’ve been, what we’ve studied, where we come from—all of that finds its way in somehow; that’s inevitable. But it’s not something we deliberately set out to pursue. The dialogue between Antonella’s electric guitar, electronics and field recordings and Renata’s dilruba, synthesizers and toys creates a fascinating balance between the ancient and the contemporary, the acoustic and the electronic. How did your different musical backgrounds shape the development of Moola, and were there particular moments during the recording process when those differences became especially productive? The most beautiful aspect of this meeting and collaboration was the complete freedom of the compositional process. Every idea was given the chance to exist, without us deciding in advance what it might become. Recordings of Orthodox ceremonies, natural landscapes, completely chaotic environments—everything was sampled, taken apart, and reassembled according to a free-flowing process rather than a predetermined plan. We never divided things into “this is the traditional part” and “this is the electronic part.” Everything passed through the same hands. Several pieces, particularly “Bridge” and “Forgotten Ritual”, suggest processes of transformation, passage and reconnection. The album often feels less concerned with composition in the traditional sense than with creating spaces for listening and reflection. Did you approach these tracks as narratives, rituals, sound environments, or something else entirely? There was never really a moment when we sat down with a list saying, “this is the ritual piece” or “this is the bridge piece.” Forgotten Ritual emerged more from a feeling than from a concept: something ceremonial, yet without any actual ceremony inside it, and we liked the idea of leaving that absence open rather than filling it. Bridge is more literal; it functions as a passage, a place where you remain for a few minutes without belonging to either side. We’re less interested in explaining what it means than in conveying that feeling of suspension. What does the name Moola mean to you, and how do you see this first release laying the foundations for where the project might go next? Moola is simply mūla, the Sanskrit word for “root.” Renata chose it, and it immediately felt right to both of us. It is also the name of one of the Vedic constellations, under whose sign Mallikarjun Mansur (an Indian singer we deeply admire) was born. In Indian folk belief, being born under the sign of mūla is not always considered auspicious and is sometimes even associated with misfortune. Yet the fact that one of the most moving and profound voices in Indian classical music was born under that sign was enough of a good omen for us. This record is more of a starting point than anything else. It is the first work we have produced together, after years of wanting to collaborate before finally making it happen. We had always been fascinated by each other’s world, by the way the other thought about music—worlds that, on paper, seem very far apart, yet revealed themselves to be remarkably close, almost naturally aligned, once we actually sat down and worked together, both in terms of taste and artistic vision. We are already writing new material, so this first release feels less like an arrival and more like a root growing underground before something emerges above the surface. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Romantic, Visceral is highly recommended for those who enjoy challenging music with semi-classical overtones and chilling stylistic pathways dominated by energetic electronic textures. Without neglecting its own originality and trippy, chameleon-like strength, this album stands as the missing link between Brendan Moeller, Burial, and Michel Portal. Endless playful and expressive sonic dialogues Romantic, Visceral by Christophe Bailleau O'Farrell   Christophe Bailleau O’Farrell is a multifaceted composer and sound researcher with a large catalog of releases, as well as skilled performances and written scores for a wide range of artistic media (theater, dance, etc.). His creative abilities are associated with a vast stylistic range, moving effortlessly from world acoustic sound ritualism to easy listening tinged with groovy atmospherics, abstract avant-gardism, and cinematic ambient with a chilling dimension. People familiar with the key indie label Mahorka have definitely heard of him, as he has published a handful of releases over the last few years. Among them, we can highlight the highly recommended album Sonic Pool Hypnose Club for its deep-listening tendencies and remarkable work on timbres, which will delight fans of drone ambient music. O’Farrell has also released several collaborative albums, notably with Julien Demoulin, Julien Ash, and Pulse Emitter for the superb, glitch-esque, Dadaesque, spacious, and dynamic Gaz Giant. I actually discovered his sound production through that release. A deeply evocative cinematic quality :: Titled Romantic, Visceral, this new album embraces the panoramic and eclectic side of Bailleau O’Farrell, especially with regard to the vast array of musical ingredients carefully combined and beautifully orchestrated. The album includes several friends and musical collaborators, such as Julien Ash, who is also responsible for the mastering. It opens with the invigorating “Malek” and its tremendous guitar-centered, Eastern-inspired synthadelic vibe, punctuated by calming, floating, then pulsating electronic patterns. This track announces the colorful, composite, and richly sonic dimensions of the album. Soothing and downtempo sequences also enter the mix, as heard in the mysteriously captivating “Fusion,” with its almost big beat-inspired groovy passages. The album delivers endless playful and expressive sonic dialogues. A deeply evocative cinematic quality is equally noticeable in the melodramatic, strange, and melodic “Phiphi, c’est toi, tu es là ?” There is a well-articulated sense of collage throughout, complementing the fractured and surreal appeal of the visual artwork. Highly recommended for those who enjoy challenging music with semi-classical overtones and chilling stylistic pathways dominated by energetic electronic textures. Without neglecting its own originality and trippy, chameleon-like strength, this album stands as the missing link between Brendan Moeller, Burial, and Michel Portal. Romantic, Visceral is available on Mahorka. [Bandcamp] Romantic, Visceral by Christophe Bailleau O'FarrellThe post Christophe Bailleau O’Farrell :: Romantic, Visceral (Mahorka) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: With The Hexadecimal Era, Sleep Underwriter delivers an album that celebrates electronic music’s past with joy and aplomb while sounding completely alive to the present moment. Here, then, is another superb release from Dublin’s Aduaine, a label whose catalog continues to set an impressively high bar through both consistency and relentless quality. A complete album that is as dancefloor-ready as it is headphone-friendly The Hexadecimal Era by Sleep Underwriter   Sleep Underwriter‘s The Hexadecimal Era makes truly wicked use of classic electronic dance music themes through contemporary production, constructing nine exhilarating cuts that effortlessly traverse electro, braindance and elements of IDM. Packed tight with immaculately programmed beats, deeply delicious synth work and an expansive set of badass, brooding basslines, it forms a complete album that is as dancefloor-ready as it is headphone-friendly. There’s a genuine sense of electronic music history running through every track. Elements of 80s synth-pop, 90s second-generation electro and nu-school electro-funk and acid intertwine with the more cerebral IDM explorations of the 2000s before embracing the genre-fluid experimentation that has defined the last decade. Rather than sounding nostalgic, Sleep Underwriter fuses these influences into something fresh, confident and unmistakably 3001 in aesthetic. Inventive sequencing and inspired sound design :: Opener “Brock” arrives big and bold, while the relentlessly ecstatic “Mud” immediately demonstrates an impressive command of arrangement, layering intricate rhythms and shifting melodic ideas with remarkable precision. Elsewhere, “Ionic Rocket” and “Bow String” channel classic 303 acid lines, reiterating the album’s desire to remain grounded in familiar territory while constantly pushing forward through inventive sequencing and inspired sound design. My standout, “Tranq Wars,” is a braindance tour de force, its complex time signatures and restless energy creating one of the album’s most enduringly rewarding moments—one I simply can’t stop replaying. Closing track “Rech” completes the journey with incredible emotional weight, where tender, emotive pads and a beautifully cinematic finale feel like the closing credits to an unforgettable, transformative voyage that fully embodies the artist’s vision. With The Hexadecimal Era, Sleep Underwriter delivers an album that celebrates electronic music’s past with joy and aplomb while sounding completely alive to the present moment. Here, then, is another superb release from Dublin’s Aduaine, a label whose catalog continues to set an impressively high bar through both consistency and relentless quality. The Hexadecimal Era is available on Aduaine. [Bandcamp] The Hexadecimal Era by Sleep UnderwriterThe post Sleep Underwriter :: The Hexadecimal Era (Aduaine) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: If hope is absent, there remains at least the desire for hope, and in that uneasy space Iron Lung and FRKSE offer an erstwhile companion as the trade winds of failing systems continue to buffet the human experiment. A necessary reality check for those who claim to be politically averse Seattle’s Iron Lung continue something uniquely their own with FRKSE‘s latest offering, Through The Slow Dusk. Here, samplers collide with traditional instrumentation and Crass-like vocal deliveries to bewail the dystopian realities of modern urban advancement through what I’d call an erudite pragmatism rather than the atonal pessimism one might first interpret experientially. Wiry tones meander over metallurgical beats, found-sound percussion and metal-bashing quotas evolve and dissolve, while the lyrical concerns encompass climate collapse, anachronistic anarchism’s potential and an almost Book of Revelation-like rapture. Through The Slow Dusk is no pleasant waltz. It is a necessary reality check for those who claim to be politically averse. In this, it becomes a sour balm for anyone who decries politics altogether, or dares not comprehend that simply getting out of bed each morning—or refusing to—is itself a political statement. We either perform with the Machine, or attempt to work within it in ways that might still benefit those around us to form a collective consciousness for change whilst there’s short-time. There is the possibility of hopelessness should we read the room if the album this way. As FRKSE states, “We’re cooked.” Yet this message arrives from the beautiful madness of the margins, clothed in the oldest Anarcho-punk ripped jeans. What becomes evident musically is the empirically expressed knowing of precisely what the artist seeks to communicate. There are no creative affectations here—only informed, frank, open-hearted and shoulder-shaking truths about the here and now, and its perhaps inevitable consequences. If hope is absent, there remains at least the desire for hope, and in that uneasy space Iron Lung and FRKSE offer an erstwhile companion as the trade winds of failing systems continue to buffet the human experiment. Through The Slow Dusk is available on Iron Lung. [Bandcamp] Through The Slow Dusk (LUNGS-314) by FRKSEThe post FRKSE :: Through The Slow Dusk (Iron Lung) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Not having fully recovered creatively after the breakup of his band The Whole Wide World, Kevin reinvented himself, much as he had when leaving Soft Machine years earlier. He assembled a group of vocalists, including the seasoned Liza Strike, and surrounded himself with friends such as Robert Wyatt, Mike Ratledge, and Steve Hillage, as well as David Bedford on orchestral arrangements; these contributions created a sound that was richer, more expansive, and less experimental, yet harmonically richer."Don't Let It Get You Down" opens with a horn section and his deep, welcoming voice. The soul influence is evident, followed by one of the album's gems, a track that highlights his singer-songwriter side (one of his greatest strengths) with intimate, heartfelt lyrics, featuring him on acoustic guitar and Steve Hillage on electric.Their distinctive take on blues and soul continues on "When Your Parents Go To Sleep," a track they always managed to imbue with an atmospheric, otherworldly quality, as if the earth itself were too small for them. The duet with Archie Leggett, who also played bass, turned out beautifully; as the preceding song put it, "you can count your friends on the fingers of one hand.""Interview" is an atonal, dystopian, and distorted blues track, ahead of its time, that paves the way for the album's most ambitious song, "Decadence." Clocking in at over eight minutes, its progression is somewhat reminiscent of "Why Are We Sleeping", that anthem he composed during his time with Soft Machine. Although uncredited, I believe Steve plays on this track too; such things happened back then, fortunately, before everything was so rigidly programmed and calculated down to the last detail. Synthesizers and guitars layer upon one another, building an atmosphere reminiscent of Gong, before concluding with an atonal piano that breaks apart.When things got too serious, Kevin needed to play around a bit; hence the inclusion of "Oh! Wot A Dream", a dreamy, pastoral melody (complete with a duck) and cozy, high-pitched guitar notes. Then there is "Hymn," a reflective track featuring piano work reminiscent of early-70s Pink Floyd, specifically the Atom Heart Mother and Meddle era, showcasing Kevin in a song-oriented mode where he was equally at home. Bananamour navigates the space between these worlds: part experimental, part song-based, with touches of soul and blues... yet 100% Kevin. It balances noise and silence, blending cryptic concepts with moments as crystal-clear as spring water."Beware Of The Dog" features orchestration by David Bedford, and it shows, masterfully closing an album that fits perfectly within the parameters for those of us who enjoy the universe created by this eternal wanderer.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Synthesizers... an army of synthesizers... the very same kind that surrounded Rick Wakeman, yet here they serve one of the founding fathers of German electronic music. They are joined by Harald Grosskopf on drums, lending the sound a more organic quality. Klaus Schulze's seventh album serves as the soundtrack to Body Love, a 1970s film by Lasse Braun. Despite the visual excesses that such a film might entail, the music ranges from the subtle to the sublime, featuring complex, elaborate, symphonic-style arrangements. It is a space epic, an outward journey that can just as easily become an inward voyage of self-discovery."Stardancer" unfolds its ideas through keyboard-generated basslines and choral sounds, all delivered with a subtlety and delicacy of arrangement that the film itself lacks. While the film exists merely to show, Schulze's album exists to suggest and to stir the imagination through its chords and notes; unlike other records, it projects its key themes like laser beams across the constellations of the universo, visible and almost tangible. There are traces of Vangelis and Pink Floyd, and a progressive concept that moves beyond naturalism in "Stardancer."Schulze's signature is there, floating in those echoes that resemble birds flying in the distance, or an endless stream of falling shooting stars... take, for instance, the unhurried track "Blanche": a distant piano begins, soon joined by layers of keyboards, they almost seem to sing! There is more melody here than on other albums, and interestingly, the mood shifts between warm and cold, blue, postmodern, glacial, metallic... It builds and raises bridges, futuristic architectural feats connecting imaginary worlds, fantasies, or nightmares, shaping that realm, as transparent as a soap bubble, that electronic music sometimes inhabits.P.T.O. reminded me of Popol Vuh, specifically the soundtrack to Werner Herzog's Aguirre, the Wrath of God, and also of the Pink Floyd of Wish You Were Here; it is as if the track fuses two virgin, elusive realms, the jungle and outer space, into a single point. The madness the English band sang about in their tribute to Syd Barrett represents that other, still-unexplored frontier into which the music ventures, much like an explorer. And therein lies, in part, the nature of this genre.Suddenly, the rhythm takes hold and the track takes flight, driven by the drums and a supporting chorus; synthesizers stretch out to fill the sky, while the drums occasionally break the rhythm to great effect. The melody circles and spirals, brushing against psychedelic hues, shifting between high, piercing peaks and contrasting deep, low notes. After all, the artist is, among other things, a brilliant composer who imbues every phrase we hear with meaning, leading to a finale that is, inevitably, cinematic in scope, yet stands apart from any visual imagery.

items.body: Review by Squonk19 — Great Journeys is the fourth album release by Riffstone, the UK, studio-based, progressive rock collaboration between those unbelievably prolific North-West musicians, Colin Powell (of A Multitude of One and Nova Cascade), and Dave Allen (of Spirergy) and in only a year. They debuted with a narrative-driven, historical concept album, Richard III and then have followed it with the impressive Sanctuary Sky and then Mythical Creatures more recently.Great Journeys is another concept-driven release exploring the spirit of human exploration - across continents, oceans, history and beyond the Earth itself. Each track represents a different journey, with Colin and Dave creating textured, cinematic, progressive rock soundscapes with layered musicianship and dense, evocative storytelling lyrics. Once again there is vibrant guitar and keyboard interplay, with balancing power and restraint, with both sharing guitar, bass, keyboard and vocals duties as usual. The result is a mix of classic-era prog with more contemporary nuances and even some accessible pop sensibilities.The album opens with The Orient Express, one of four tracks written and performed by Colin, with the other tracks more collaborative efforts with Dave. Beginning with the sound of a steam train and then programmed drumming as the journey begins, the song mixes piano motifs, keyboard chords and subtle guitar lines over Colin's light vocals, picking up the pace until the end. Dave joins Colin on the Far Eastern-tinged, The Silk Road, which has some nice, gutsy guitar playing and probing bass. The atmospheric instrumental, Himalayas, is an undoubted highlight, evoking the mountainous, high-altitude vistas well, with soaring synthesisers aplenty, and some well-judged guitar soloing later.Camino de Santiago takes us on the ancient, Iberian pilgrimage trail, with some stately orchestrated choral effects and electric guitar contrasting with bright acoustic guitar and Colin's faster, almost singalong-style vocals. South Pole is one of two longer epics from Colin, with a more desolate and restrained pace. The varied, flowing and atmospheric instrumentation supports the wind-swept, cold weariness of the vocals, with the repeating piano and bass guitar lines particularly effective. The Voyage of the Beagle takes us on the exploratory journeys of Charles Darwin across the southern oceans and is a refreshing contrast, full of swirling Wakeman-like keyboards, expressive guitar and Dave's yearning, higher register vocals a foil to those of Colin later.Mariana takes us into the dark depths of the Pacific Ocean and has a suitably slow, cinematic sweep, with background keyboard chords over restrained stabs of piano and acoustic guitar, and Dave's dreamlike vocals. The rhythm picks up, with undulating synthesisers appearing later. Red Horizon is the second of Colin's longer epics and is another album highlight. Starting with a suitably majestic, orchestrated fanfare, the imagined trip to Mars is a diverse track with a sprightly, repeating chorus threading through more sleepy and lush instrumentation. The tempo rises and falls throughout with more expressive keyboards and some nice electric guitar later, with Colin pushing his vocals to more varied styles as well. The album ends on a more melancholic and wistful note with The Maps Are Fading To White, as piano patterns and orchestrated strings accompany the thoughts of an older explorer pondering the many journeys and their meaning (in many ways I thought of Rutger Hauer's Tears in Rain monologue from Bladerunner at times). This low-key ending works surprisingly well.With four albums in a year from Riffstone, many might be concerned that quantity might be affecting quality, but whilst Great Journeys is not breaking any new ground and is definitely anchored in their previous instrumental and vocal signature style, it is a worthy addition to this talented duo's collection of works. The concept is an engaging one, and there are sufficient points of musical interest to keep fans of their previous albums satisfied. The CD artwork is as charming as ever, with images of Colin and Dave on their various travels, and is but one of many reasons to keep this grass-roots prog cottage industry going, as long as their ideas and inspiration remain fresh.(from The Progressive Aspect - A Different Aspect 100)

items.body: Review by Squonk19 — Mythical Creatures is the third album release by Riffstone, the UK, studio-based, progressive rock collaboration between those prolific North-West musicians, Dave Allen (of Spirergy) and Colin Powell (of A Multitude of One and Nova Cascade), in under a year. They debuted with a bold, narrative-driven, historical concept album, Richard III and then followed it up at the end of last year with the impressive Sanctuary Sky. That was a refreshingly diverse collection of songs, full of instrumental and lyrical interplay and musicianship of the highest quality - and was one of the highlights of the year for me. If that wasn't enough, Colin managed to produce two lovely concept albums last year under his solo project name, A Multitude of One: A Templar's Tale and The Book of Enoch - whilst Dave released the excellent Wherever Forever album at the start of this year under the Spirergy project name. Just how brimming full of musical ideas this duo have is quite astonishing!Mythical Creatures sees a return to the concept album approach, with each of the ten songs linked to a creature from mythology. Each of these legendary creatures are featured, to symbolise and represent psychological forces that act as mirrors for the human psyche. The lyrics convey this deeper meaning, whilst the music creates rich, cinematic, symphonic progressive rock soundscapes, with layered musicianship and wonderfully vibrant guitar and keyboard interplay. As before, they share guitar, keyboard and vocals between them, creating their now signature sound - embracing the classic sound of Yes, Genesis, Camel, Rick Wakeman, ELP, Steve Hackett and Alan Parsons, but with nods to more contemporary groups, such as Big Big train as well. All the tracks have expansive instrumental passages, with shifting time signatures and dynamic contrasts, along with atmospheric mid-sections balanced with powerful choruses. The result blends power and restraint, with soaring hooks and dramatic climaxes aplenty.The Griffin begins the album energetically, with keyboards and undulating bass and drums accompanying Dave's descriptive vocals about this half eagle, half lion creature, depicting balance and integrated strength. Well-integrated electric guitar joins the shifting instrumentation later, with some powerful soloing towards the end. The Dragon represents ambition and fire and has a stately Rick Wakeman-like keyboard/synthesiser character throughout, over the driving bass and busy drum programming, with lots of Moog-like passages to delight classic-era prog listeners.Soaring, ethereal vocal harmonies begin The Phoenix, with atmospheric acoustic guitar lines over a lush keyboard background and then a gorgeous electric guitar solo that heralds a rise in intensity and dynamics, with twisting bass notes. Dave's higher vocals have an accessible AOR feel to them, whilst a mid-way interlude of more Spanish guitar serves as a prelude to a powerful finale and more invigorating guitar soloing. By contrast, Colin's dark, sinister and distorted vocals provide a stylistic variation on The Hydra. The subject of internal conflict is well represented, with intricate and varied instrumental interplaying of keyboards, guitar and bass between the pair creating a foreboding ambience, but not without the odd uplifting light shining amongst the dark elements. As a result, it wouldn't be out of place on an IQ album at times, in my opinion.The crowned serpent is the subject of The Basilisk - represents paralysing awareness. The music conjures up a feeling of dread, accentuated by the pair's yearning vocals, with repeating guitar patterns, expansive organ passages and a slower rhythm adding to the mix. An eerie dancing tempo appears, followed by a spoken word passage and then some rising synths before you join a Cabaret-like march towards your fate. The Manticore follows and is an undoubted album highlight. Starting urgently, and at times having a dark, almost metal-like, intensity - it gradually shifts into Floydian keyboard soundscapes and mellotron-like dreaminess. I enjoyed the more modern, electronic elements too, earlier on. This track looks at distorted power - charisma fused with cruelty and confidence sharpened into domination - something which certainly resonates with me at present, in the current geo-political climate. Colin delivers more dark vocals to great effect as well as adding an innocent delicacy to the main lyrics, through to the contemplative "I am YOU!" There is an initial Celtic folk edge to The Selkies, with its sprightly piano opening, but it first switches into a more rock-orientated sound, and then a more lyrical and melodic, dreamy ambience supplied by the electric guitar. The dynamics build up again later, with vibrant bass guitar, expressive keyboards and intricate guitar lines - which along with Dave's ethereal vocals, produce an enjoyable Yes-like vibe. These seal-folk of the northern seas, represent dual identity and longing - changing from seals to humans by shedding their skins. The track musically shows this dual nature of them living on the land but also longing to return to the sea. The track explores this dichotomy within them, and considers the wider question of what happens when belonging to two worlds means never fully resting in either? Meanwhile, The Chimera reflects on fragmentation and inner conflict, with its separate identities of lion, goat, and serpent fused into an uneasy entity. The track has a flowing grandeur and majesty, with lush keyboards in the background, over which Dave and Colin weave a tapestry of melodic guitar, bass and synths. Dave's vocals seem to soar high beyond the stratosphere at times, but they seem to add to the overall splendour. Electric guitar takes centre stage at the start of The Leviathan, the vast sea serpent of chaos, symbolising the subconscious vastness - ancient memory, collective shadow and emotional magnitude beyond language. However, it is the wonderfully melodic bass playing that drives this smooth piece of symphonic progressive rock. Its another song that has a gravitas and weight shaped by the duo in their flowing instrumentation, complemented by Colin's soft vocals. The final track, The Unicorn, is lighter and more uplifting, with Yes-like vocal harmonies from Colin and Dave and sumptuous musicality. The synthesised flights of fancy are perfect for this song representing restored wholeness ? innocence and purity. Acoustic guitar lines and a welcoming lightness of touch with the drums and bass create something unashamedly retro in its shining brightness - and a lovely, positive, life-affirming way to end the album. With Riffstone, Dave Allen and Colin Powell may not be creating anything radically new. However, they are producing wonderfully melodic, warm and engaging traditional symphonic prog rock, showcasing their compositional and instrumental skills along with engaging lyrics and a pleasing innocence in their floating vocal arrangements. It is music they clearly love and I've no doubt that many out there will love it too. With the excellent CD artwork and care to detail throughout, and just under 80 minutes of music, this grass-roots contribution to the world of prog certainly deserves your patronage via Bandcamp.(from Progressive Voyages)

items.body: Review by Warthur — Zappa might have been a musical perfectionist, and he might have been able to exert significantcreative control in the studio, but when it comes to movie-making nobody, not even a Kubrick-likeauteur, can accomplish much without collaborators. The tension between Zappa and other members ofthe cast and crew was widely-reported on at the time and seems to flourish from time to timeonscreen; Zappa himself is an almost invisible presence, appearing only in the band segments andinstead represented by Ringo Starr as "Larry the Dwarf", or as a highly unrealistic dummy - adecision which might have also made it easier when people weren't getting on with him and hits onthe movie's most convincing thematic element, depicting the band as becoming more and more paranoidunder Zappa's covert surveillance.But even though the movie has its better moments, it's trying to do altogether too much at once. Youcan cram lots of musical ideas into a single composition and make them work, of course - Zappa'swhole musical schtick is based on that. When it comes to movie-making, though, trying to do too muchat once is a peril that has upended far more polished productions than this.The extensive use of video effects, which helped it stand out the time, has dated poorly, but thereal giveaway is the problem with the aspect ratio. Watch it in 16:9, and most of the scenes areproperly framed but the band performances and other moments are zoomed-in to an almost uncomfortableextent. Watch it in 4:3, and at least one effects shot is completely ruined. In other words, themovie has all the telltale signs of being shot without a clear idea of what the actual aspect ratiowas going to be from the start.The music is grand. But the visuals don't add as much to the music as you might expect, and if youhave the soundtrack album and haven't watched the movie the version in your head may well be betterthan what's on screen.

items.body: Review by Warthur — I said when I reviewed the CD version of this Pallas release that it might well be the band's finesthour - a show that stands head and shoulders not just all their other live offerings, but also theirstudio output. The visuals of the show do not disappoint, with Alan Reed's theatrics judgedcarefully to always add to rather than distract from his vocal performance and the rest of the bandon top form.The stage setup and the use of light is also well judged - here is a band which never quite made theleap from clubs full of passionate fans to arena glory the way their peers in Marillion did, but onewhich has as a consequence made the best of the constraints they are in, creating a sense of beingushered into a dark subterranean temple - appropriately given the heavy use of material from TheCross and the Crucible. And Euan Lowson's guest appearance at the end makes this one of the few(only?) sources to actually see his style as a frontman, including the return of the truly over thetop theatrics on The Ripper which made that such an electrifying and controversial feature of theirearly setlist.

items.body: You carry the weight at night No secrets in the light There’s nowhere left to hide Exposed in the day exposed in the night Rani Sharone’s dark alternative solo project And it was Night presents What’s Beyond the Light? as a nocturnal crossing where landscape, memory, and perception keep changing places. Written after moonlit walks and drawing from The Cure, Echo and the Bunnymen, The Church, My Bloody Valentine, and The Mission, the song moves with a steady club pulse while guitars dissolve at the edges and electronics cast a dim, narcotic sheen across the mix. Beneath its poised surface lies a persistent unease, as though each familiar street has shifted from where it stood yesterday. That dislocation becomes the governing principle of the accompanying video, filmed and edited by Sharone himself. Wandering through open terrain, climbing stairs, and performing amid blurred natural forms, he places the body inside unstable spaces. Glitches rupture the image, repeated gestures lose their ordinary meaning, and forward motion begins to feel circular. The camera keeps seeking an exit while the edit folds the route back into itself. What begins as an evening walk gradually assumes the character of a private trial, with every path offering revelation and misdirection in equal measure. The video’s strongest passages come from its willingness to let simple actions acquire psychological weight. A staircase becomes a threshold without a promised destination. Trees and roadside textures appear less as scenery than as active witnesses. Familiar locations are altered through framing, repetition, and digital fracture until the everyday begins to look conspiratorial. The song’s guide through darkness may offer companionship, yet the images preserve uncertainty about where the journey leads and whether illumination can be trusted. Sharone’s performance is embedded within the montage rather than elevated above it, which suits a song concerned with guidance, doubt, and perception slipping out of alignment. The visual language draws from experimental music television, home-video abstraction, and the soft distortions of a dream recalled too quickly after waking. “Short form videos have always proved to be a fun and creative way to give my music a visual pairing, so jumping into a full length video was an amazing exercise and challenge,” says Sharone. “I set out to create a dreamy and sometimes disorienting video filled with movement, nature, and things that directly inspired my lyrics for the song, including sights from my own neighborhood.” Watch the video for “What’s Beyond the Light?” below: Rani Sharone’s wider career supplies useful context without overwhelming the work: he has toured and recorded with Puscifer and Stolen Babies, collaborated with film composers, written for animation, and contributed to the music team behind K-Pop Demon Hunters. Here, those experiences converge in pop whose visual imagination carries the greatest force, turning a moonlit walk into a restless study of desire, fear, and the unreliable architecture of night. Listen to What’s Beyond The Light? below and order the single here. items.body: For more than two decades, IAMX, the solo project of artist Chris Corner, has occupied a singular, ineffable space within dark and alternative music, while at the same time managing to bend and penetrate genres outside the scene. IAMX returns to Europe this summer for the Recollections Tour, with special appearances at festivals including M’era Luna, Infest, and Extramuralhas, alongside a run of headline dates across more unusual territories, including the Nordic countries, Türkiye, and others to be confirmed. Fans can find tickets to all shows on the IAMX website. A highlight of the run is a double-night invasion of Stockholm. The band will perform their infamous, electrifying, high-octane set one night, while also offering a super unique acoustic set and mental health gathering on another. Set against a backdrop of high-art stage design and bombastic rave visuals, the main set will include revamped beloved IAMX classics not heard for years, along with heavier live versions of recent albums. Held the evening before, the acoustic gathering offers honest conversations about mental health, neurodiversity, and sexuality, interwoven with stripped-back acoustic performances of IAMX songs. Ahead of their first shows, Corner and IAMX live band member Gözde Düzer, known for her own fantastic, gritty hauntwave solo project Aux Animaux, turn the spotlight on one another for their own intimate conversation over a few glasses of wine. Their discussion travels from the evolution of IAMX to mental health and neurodiversity, and finding connection in an increasingly fractured world. Photo by Kris Sulekova Gözde: After a period of intense focus on the Fault Lines era, we’re going to be doing this tour focused a bit more on older songs. How does it feel to move into a retrospective realm? Chris: It feels bizarre and amazing at the same time. I felt like the Fault Lines thing dragged on, really, because a lot of personal stuff dragged on. What was happening in my personal life and those two albums seemed so intertwined with each other that they both felt like the same thing in an odd way. Moving into this retrospective thing, I am ready to write new material, but not quite. My head is still stuck on a personal level. I’m trying to shake myself up, and I think doing this retrospective thing gives me a bit of breathing space, but also allows me to be playful with old stuff and have some fun and give people what they want, and not be too serious. Because writing is serious. If I start fully going into the writing mode right now, I think it would just probably be too intense. There’s a certain lightness to retrospective stuff that, you know, it’s done, it’s accepted, and I can play with it and have fun with it, and not worry too much about what I’m trying to say. It’s all been said, really. It’s a bit weird, but mostly it feels perfect, timing-wise. Gözde: I think it’s also great bringing the hits to the festival shows. And also the way we play them on stage isn’t like the album version because you redo all the songs for a live performance. Everything is always being reworked in some way. One version we played in the spring might not even be the same on the stage on these summer shows, right? It’s still new and exciting. Chris: That’s part of it. Initially, it needs to be fun and cool and interesting to me. If I take an old song, I don’t want to just live with it as it was. It’s not interesting to me anymore. It’s more like, what can I do with it now, and how can I present it in a slightly more modern way? My production techniques have changed over the years, and my priorities and my sound have developed. To take an old track, I would never just do it as it was. I mean, it still has that feeling. A song is written in a certain way, you can’t extract that completely, but it is fun for me to rework it. Otherwise, I probably wouldn’t ever listen to that thing ever again. When I’ve written and produced and recorded and finished and completed and put it out, and been through the whole exposure therapy of putting art out, there’s a lot of pleasure. But there’s also a lot of self-doubt and questions. It’s never complete. I mean, that feeling, every artist has it, I’m absolutely certain. There is no perfect product. Having a second chance, that’s what I like about live stuff too, is you have many chances. You can keep improving it, and you can keep getting it better–or what you think is better, of course. Everybody has, it’s very subjective. Somebody who’s super focused on the original version of “Kiss + Swallow” from the first album might be offended by adding a new snare sound or something. I’m not. And that keeps my engine running. Gözde: That makes sense. I remember reading about Nirvana and that Kurt Cobain didn’t want to play “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” and maybe that was part of the reason why, because the album version is already super clean, and it almost doesn’t sound like that raw Nirvana sound. And then they have to play the song over and over again. But when you do something like you do, the song progresses with you, especially in a live setting, because that’s also different from the recorded version, that also keeps the song exciting for the performer too. When we play some of the IAMX songs on stage, they almost feel a bit metal. When we go all in with live drums and the bass and all… Photo by Kris Sulekova Chris: The live part of IAMX has really brought out that energy and harshness and rawness that sometimes I don’t quite achieve on the records, because my head isn’t there.When you’re making a record, you have all of these technical concerns. Your energy is very different. Your mood is different. You’re a bit more subdued, maybe. The live experience – not just for the person on stage, but for the listener, the audience too – there’s an energy that’s quite difficult to recreate in the studio. Particularly if you’re doing it yourself, like I do. You can’t always project your mind into that space, and your body, and your voice. Often it would be ideal to play the record for a whole year live and then record it, you know, like they used to do. Gözde: I think about that a lot too. Now, when I start playing the new songs live before releasing them with Aux Animaux, I realize that it was actually much better to do so, because then, even with the vocals, you come up with other stuff you wouldn’t in the studio. There’s something liberating about performing them in a live setting and then going back to the studio with whatever emerged. Chris: Exactly. And there’s a certain limit to what you can achieve in a certain time as well. You can live and breathe and experience things and see people’s reactions and see, “Oh, they like that. They don’t like that.” Or, “This worked. That worked. I felt good when I did that. My voice got stronger.” There’s too many variables. You can’t express that fully in a studio environment, particularly for the music that we do. If there’s a full band bashing away for two weeks, maybe. We’re not that. But I do love the idea of the metal energy element, and that’s something that I’m flirting with bringing into the sound, for sure. Gözde: Right! Do you mean bringing in the metal sound on the records as well? Chris: I keep coming back to this idea that there has to be an IAMX hybrid mutant metal record. I have no idea how I’ll do it, but I’ll find a way. I think it’s gonna happen. I know it. Gözde: I think it totally should! I was thinking about that the other day when I went to see the A Perfect Circle show, and then I asked you, “When are we gonna do that metal album?” Chris: I know. I come back to that feeling too. It’s odd because metal is so connected with a load of dudes on stage doing this thing. Trying to extract that energy, and formulate that into a weird electronic studio environment is a challenge. It would be really interesting if I could somehow make that. I mean, a lot of industrial stuff has that energy too. It has been done in that sense. But with IAMX it’s a different beast. Let’s see what I can do. Gözde: That’s gonna be really cool. I’m looking forward to that! By the way, going back to the highlights, “Bernadette” has exploded over the past few years to become one of the most popular IAMX songs. The single is being re-released on vinyl this summer just ahead of the tour. What do you think it is about “Bernadette” that has resonated with so many people? Chris: Obviously because it’s a really hardcore metal tune! No, it’s the least metal IAMX song ever. Who knows? I mean, there are tracks that I’ve done with different projects–my previous band–that people gravitate to. There are IAMX songs that people gravitate to. The stuff that I like is not the stuff that others like. I don’t have the answer to any of that. I’m not a pop producer or writer. I’ve never really gone into any writing process with that in mind. I’ve always found it very fragile that when people go into, at least with the people that I’ve worked with who are obviously not pop writers, when you go into that thinking, “I’m going to write a commercial song,” you’re setting yourself up for failure. I don’t know what that is. With “Bernadette,” the one thing that I remember when I wrote it, was that it was a very concentrated song. I spent a lot of time crafting it. The chord changes were very different to what I was doing at the time. I pushed things. It was a very songy-song. That’s all I can say. There’s a lot of genuine emotion in it. It’s quite simple. But then there are other IAMX songs that are simple too. I don’t know what the thing is there. It’s definitely a special song. It’s got a special thing. You can sing it like a simple song. It’s got a girl’s name. You know, the thing. It hits certain buttons that the human storytelling condition likes. You could sit around the campfire and talk about “Bernadette.” There’s a storyline to it. It has a bit of a narrative, I guess. I don’t know. Photo by Kris Sulekova Gözde: Sometimes it’s also like you just write this song from your own perspective, in your own little world, and then you put it out there for people to do whatever they want with it. And then, I guess they relate more to some songs, for reasons unknown. The song starts to have a life of its own. It makes its own path. Chris: It is on its own path. And it’s not just a relational path. It’s also a cultural path. Timing. Things that happened around it. You really can’t predict that. The only thing I can think of that has ever made any sense is when something has felt so intense and right to me that I just know it’s going to feel right to somebody else. That’s the only thing. And I have that with every song, of course. We all do. But some of those feelings last and some of them don’t. Some of them are in the moment. It’s like, “Okay, the reason why that works is because the beat was really heavy, and that feels great, and I could imagine being in a club and just losing my shit.” That’s amazing. It’s a great feeling. And it might last. But that might change next year when techno comes in, or whatever. But there’s a certain thing about a certain relational emotion that you write into a song that–I really think that if it means something true, it’s going to mean something true to somebody else. Gözde: We’ll be hosting a mental health gathering for fans with acoustic performances in August in Stockholm. It’s been several years since IAMX had a mental health gathering before a live show, and that’s going to be the first time for me doing that mental health thing with IAMX. Can you tell me a little bit about it? What is it exactly? Chris: It’s basically a safe space where we can all get in a room, be a certain accepted, weird, neurodiverse cult, and bring our challenges and our awe to the table and share it. Just talk. It’s like communion. It’s something that I know I need. It’s a selfish project, to be honest. I started it post-breakdown, when I’d had a few years of my own difficult mental health challenges. I found it super comforting and productive to start that and to do it, and to share the things that I had learned about myself, and about psychology, and therapy, and all of these tools that I had learned to restabilize myself. It was beautiful as well because it’s not just a dry therapeutic situation. It’s a very unique situation because you have an artist and the listener, and you can connect about life, but also about the art. You can go deeper into the art. I can learn things about myself, but also about them, how they experience me, how they experience my work. It’s really unique. At some point, I just felt like music, visuals, and the video, and everything, it just wasn’t enough. I was like, I’m in this world, and I’m human, and I’m socially awkward, and I don’t relate very well, but I’m desperate to relate even though I can’t. On a personal level, it’s been difficult. There were all these different moving parts. Then there’s this whole–there are thousands and thousands of people out there that accept and love me. I was like, “Well, how the fuck do I get to them on an intimate level?” Not just through social media and stuff like that. How do I sit in a room and use that energy that we both would like to use? That seemed to be a good place to do it. I’ve really missed it. It stopped for a while because life happened, and things changed, and lots of transitions, and then the pandemic happened. Here we are, five years later. It’s like, “Oh my God, I need to get back and do that shit because it was amazing.” It’s selfish, but it’s also a certain duty. One of the keys to positive and healthy mental health is to look outside yourself. To connect with others. To diminish your own ego. You can go out into nature and experience nature, and that brings your ego down. What else do you do? You get to know other people. You listen to them. You talk to them. You get to know their stories. I’m a super curious person. I love to know about others. But I need a safe environment for that because I’m also an autistic person. It’s socially sticky for me to formulate the right environment for me to do that. It’s a perfect place for me. It’s a weird corrupted social environment. I really hope to release it sometime this summer if I can finish mixing the song.§ Chris & Gözde The conversation above follows up on an exchange Post-Punk.com began with Corner last August, ahead of IAMX’s 2025 Fault Lines² North American Tour. In that earlier interview, Corner spoke about IAMX’s first performance in New Orleans, the evolving role of Silent Valley Studios, HEADNOISE, autism, polyamory, AI’s pressure on artists and audiences, obsession as a creative engine, and the practical limits of mounting an independent tour. The discussion also reached the relationship between grief and “The Ocean,” the visual dimension of Corner’s work, and the deeper album tracks he would place on an IAMX starter mixtape. IAMX opened 2026 with “Artificial Innocence” on February 20, a new single that later appeared in two forms on the UNMASK EP: the original recording and the extended “UNMASK Mix.” Released digitally on May 22 after first being sold exclusively on the 2025 Fault Lines² European Tour, UNMASK gathers five pieces from the Fault Lines period: “Grass Before The Scythe (ArtBleedsMoney Rework),” “Artificial Innocence (UNMASK Mix),” “Radical Self Love,” “There Will Be Times When I Will Need To Hurt You,” and “Artificial Innocence.” The same day brought IAMIXED: Reworks Fault Lines Albums 1 And 2 to digital platforms after its original physical-only appearance on the 2025 North American tour. The nine-track collection hands material from both Fault Lines albums to Mimetic Hexes, Holy Braille, Damn The Witch Siren, Nigen, Carrellee, clubdrugs, and ArtBleedsMoney, and includes IAMX’s orchestral rework of “War Of Words.” On May 25, “The Background Noise {Orchestral Rework}” recast the Metanoia song in a strings-led arrangement. This summer, the Bernadette EP receives its first vinyl edition, collecting seven variations on the song, including its original recording, the ArtBleedsMoney rework, an acoustic rendition, the German radio edit, “Post Romanian Storm,” “Headfuck Collage,” and an instrumental version. Those releases now feed into the Recollections Tour, which brings earlier IAMX favorites, recent material, and newly rebuilt versions into the same set. items.body: American boyhood can resemble a long induction into somebody else’s war. Strength is measured by the ability to make others submit; tenderness is seen as a liability; and young men learn to police one another before an employer, institution, or army ever needs to intervene. On “Victory in Death,” avant-garde darkwave project Mellow Code follows those instructions toward their brutal conclusion, confronting a model of masculinity designed to turn human beings into obedient bodies molded into the perfect vessels for capitalist greed and imperial power. Led by Josh McVety and Oliver Michael German, Mellow Code opens the track with deep, processional drums and a funereal mass of synthesizers. Buzzing, bit-crushed electronics churn across the upper register while shuddering samples keep the arrangement under strain. McVety’s resonant vocal booms from a distance, suspended somewhere between lament and military command. The track draws upon the physical machinery of early industrial music, but feels colder than EBM and graver than conventional darkwave. The body here is already bleeding out on the battlefield, with the genre’s flag lowered to half-mast. Repeated orders to “force it down” and “fall in line” turn masculinity into drill practice, while “just be a man” becomes both a taunt and a test whose only reward is further obedience. Even the title’s promised victory requires a form of self-erasure. Mellow Code explains: “Victory in death is a song evoking the feeling of growing up the way American culture targets boys. Preparation to be used as bodies for capital and imperialism. Fortify yourself little kid and don’t show weakness, that would be feminine or gay. Perpetuated in a cycle of abuse, boys police each other and the most conservative minded lash out at the perceived threats to that sense of “natural order”. Advertisements use the essence of porn and evoke rugged individualism to sell things but also that idea. The manosphere is only the newest mutant to spawn from this toxic path. These things feel inevitable at times but it’s not. Community and human contact is essential to humans, as is creating art. Sports are the most acceptable forms of community that also allow for some structured contact for young men. That’s why growing up as a soft art boy or boy adjacent can be hard. But if you’re lucky you find the other-ed and make art that speaks to rebellion against status quo gender existentialist bull shit. Maybe help some realize they also feel trapped by those structures.” Shot in the high desert, the accompanying video turns that critique into an unruly nocturnal workshop. Around a campfire, a gang dressed in leather, mesh, workwear, and smeared makeup saws, drills, sands, and paints pieces of wood into oversized mallets, spears, and toy-like projectiles. Those scenes are intercut with McVety, sporting a yellow mullet and delivering the song from the cold white interior of a van, a knife resting in his hand. Soon, a red-lit pickup carries the crew across the scrub with an enormous handmade slingshot mounted to its bed. Their target is a brightly painted wooden male dummy, equal parts carnival attraction, military mascot, and childhood invention. The friends bombard it with their homemade arsenal before closing in with clubs and axes, collectively demolishing the figure that has been built to represent inherited ideas of manhood. Orange firelight, hard headlights, flying sparks, and icy interior lighting give the desert escapade the character of a pirate raid organized by art-school outcasts. For McVety, the production returned to the reckless ingenuity of childhood while placing that freedom in the hands of his closest creative community: “This video was an absolute labor of love that was entirely done with and by my community of artist friends. I wanted to recapture what it felt like to be a kid when me and my freak friends would make weapons and contraptions and forts inspired by whatever movie we had just seen and often Jack Ass. Whatever felt Rad as Hell then still holds true. We built weapons and made a truck into a giant slingshot. I made a wooden dummy and my friends painted it. It was a party in the desert with the people closest to me.” The video was photographed and co-directed by Adrian Stucker of Melankolia, with Daniel Maggio serving as co-director and editor. It stars Josh McVety, Eli Gray, Matt Hanson, Miranda Sharp, and Eric Runner, with color by Grady Colors. Watch the video for “Victory in Death” below: On creating the video for Victory in Death, Adrian Stucker discusses the film’s high-desert production and the internal conflict represented by its handmade weaponry: “Serving as both Co-Director and Director of Photography for Mellow Code’s “Victory in Death,” I had the opportunity to craft a fantastically fun and highly conceptual visual narrative. The creative direction tied together the rebellious, youthful energy of The Lost Boys with the rugged, weathered aesthetic of desert-faring pirates. Shooting out in the high desert always presents its own unique environmental and logistical challenges, but the cinematic payout is consistently worth the effort. To ground the raw aesthetic of the environment, I frequently utilized a hard, single lighting source, carving out striking, high-contrast imagery against the barren landscape. Drawing directly from Mellow Code’s actual thematic focus on fabricating custom instruments and devices, we wove that maker-centric vibe deeply into the video. The narrative visually documents the meticulous process of crafting tools from other tools, which are eventually forged into weapons. However, the story intentionally subverts the traditional use of these weapons. Instead of directing this arsenal outward at enemies, the weapons are turned inward for a deeply personal fight. The core of the video captures Mellow Code on a mission to confront and metaphorically slaughter his own preconceived notions of masculinity. It is a visual exploration of dismantling internal barriers, illustrating that the most important battles are often fought within ourselves, ultimately making room to replace those outdated notions with the strength and love of the surrounding community.” For Maggio, the concept also provided an opportunity to place McVety’s skills as a carpenter and fabricator directly before the camera: “I love working with Josh. Not only does he make this wonderful, dark, hypnotic music, but he is also a master builder. He’s a brilliant carpenter who can create pretty much anything he designs. The opening shot of FACE IT (the last video we did together) is a handmade illuminated pentagram. He seemed to have made it in his spare time. I was blown away by the detail and its functionality. What can’t this guy do? For the second video, I was curious how far we could push his talents as a craftsman. He runs a shop in Alhambra and naturally works with an extremely talented, fashionable, and hardworking team. Every handmade object featured in the music video was created by the on-camera talent. You can tell they are all friends who share a professional working relationship. One of the highlights was the slingshot mounted to the top of the pickup truck. Our first launch was unsuccessful, and my fondest memory of the shoot was watching 4 cross-faded engineers troubleshoot this thing. I hope it’s as much fun to watch as it was to shoot.” Listen to “Victory in Death” below, and order the single here. Victory In Death by Mellow Code Mellow Code is an avant-garde darkwave project led by Josh McVety and Oliver Michael German. Mechanical rhythms, new-wave vocals, EBM, house, and bright FM synthesis converge with samples gathered from the group’s fabrication workshop. The recent album Object Reality, along with tracks such as “Ich stehe im Blut” and “Face It,” develops an industrial club language in which handmade devices function as instruments, images, and extensions of the music itself. Follow Mellow Code: Facebook Instagram Spotify Bandcamp The post LA Darkwave Project Mellow Code Rebels Against the Machinery of Toxic Masculinity in Video for “Victory in Death” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Band: Genghis Tron | Album: Signal Fire | Genre: Post-metal, Industrial, Cybergrind | Year: 2026 From: Poughkeepsie, USA | Label: Relapse For fans of: Dillinger Escape Plan, Nine Inch Nails, BTBAM Bandcamp Genghis Tron’s last album, 2021’s Dream Weapon, was my introduction to the band. It was also a rather sharp break with their first two records. Where their first two were scourging mixtures of electronica, grindcore, and mathcore, the lush textures and restrained tempos of Dream Weapon were downright relaxing by comparison. Their new album, Signal Fire, then, is something of a return to their earlier sound. It’s not entirely without the spacey post-rock elements that dominate on Dream Weapon, but this is a much more intense and aggressive release. “I Am All” kicks the album off with a staccato synth pattern and a sense of urgency. I’m not nuts about the unclean vocals on stretches of this song. It’s a style common in many genres of metal that end in -core, and that’s simply not something I like. In the context of the music, though, I would consider it an effective choice. I really enjoy the way the textures evolve, gradually becoming more oppressive and anxious. The title track comes next, an upbeat, sub-two-minute piece. There’s a punky, garage rock energy to this song that I love, along with some very fun, unorthodox chords and riffs. Coming straight out of that is “Future Worship”. This piece is more akin to the material on Dream Weapon, but a bit heavier. It’s melodic and synth-fueled, with some beautiful lead guitar lines. “Like Fotochrom” is another short piece, this one centered on looping, echoing synths. After that brief and relaxing interlude, “Tomorrow Mirage” explodes with screams and distorted keys and guitars. Industrial synths buzz harshly over a thumping drum pattern, and the way the band gradually ups the intensity is impressive. The music is furious, desperate, and absolutely crushing. In the song’s second half, things slow down and the piece becomes a mournful bit of electronic rock. “Nothing Blooms in the Hollow” sees the band’s fury come roaring back, this time in a context rooted more in rock and metal, rather than industrial and electronica. Traces of classic space rock acts like Hawkwind are noticeable, and the band does a great job at varying textures and dynamics as this piece progresses. I especially love the percussion in the second half of the song. “Without Form” offers a much-needed breather after that pair of absolutely pummeling compositions. A throbbing synth pulse provides just enough momentum to keep it moving as synth pads bubble in the background. And boy is it good we got that breather, because “Born Prey” pulls no punches in its opening moments, immediately assaulting the listener with black metal-tinged riffage and tortured screams. This mood doesn’t persist for the whole song; things eventually do slow down. The tempo moves from an uncompromising tornado to a steady march driven by growling bass and atmospheric synthesizers. This song becomes increasingly electronic as it progresses, ending up in a beautiful place with multi-part vocal arrangements and relatively warm synth tones. After a brief, relatively calm intro, “A Love So Pure” returns to the band’s cybergrind roots. Mathcore riffs and occasional synth inclusions make for a tense and suffocating experience. The album concludes with “New Gods”. Its opening reminds me of certain Steven Wilson songs, with its moody and minimal electronic backing and cynical lyrics. As it progresses, this song continues to draw melodically from synthpop, albeit in a minor-key and downcast form. Signal Fire, in many ways, is a more mature version of Genghis Tron’s first two records. I don’t particularly like those first two releases (see my above-noted distaste for more “-core” subgenres), so this maturation and diversification of their sound is much-welcomed. Overall, I enjoyed this record more than I expected I would based on the very first moments of it. There’s a clever blend of crushing metal and interstellar synth patterns, as well as some other further-afield inclusions. I still prefer Dream Weapon over this, but it’s pretty solid. Score: 82/100

items.body: UPDATE: the Space Craft festival was canceled Steve Roach had confirmed two live dates for August 2026: “Space Craft” in Joshua Tree, California, on August 14-15, and “Soundquest Festival” in Tucson, Arizona, on August 28-30. Both events place the dark-ambient artist alongside a wider electronic and ambient lineup. The Space Craft is canceled though. Tour dates for Steve Roach August 14-15, 2026 – Space Craft, Pioneertown, Joshua Tree, CA – with Tangerine Dream, ESG, Laraaji, Soriah, Ami Dang, Nailah Hunter and Flore Laurentienne August 28-30, 2026 – Soundquest Festival, La Rosa, Tucson, AZ – with Blood Incantation, Pallbearer, Giuseppe Ottaviani, Soriah, Karima Walker and others Space Craft was a two-night event built around the Perseid meteor shower, combining live performances with stargazing, space talks and storytelling under the night skies of the Mojave Desert. Roach was supposed to perform on the Friday, August 14 bill alongside ESG, Soriah and Ami Dang; Tangerine Dream was to headline the Saturday program with Evicshen. Tickets for Space Craft ranged from $110 to $265. At Soundquest Festival in Tucson, Roach presents “At the Edge of Forever” on Saturday, August 29, preceded by an artist meet-and-greet, and closes the weekend on Sunday, August 30 with a seated set alongside Paul Riedl, Serena Gabriel, Jeff Greinke and Linda Kohanov as part of the festival’s “Sacred Sunday” program. Tickets are available through Eventim and Vivid Seats. About Steve Roach Steve Roach is a California-born, Arizona-based composer working in dark ambient and electronic music since the early 1980s, when albums such as “Structures from Silence” (1984) established the extended, immersive style that has defined his catalogue since. He has released dozens of solo albums on his own Timeroom Editions label and through Projekt Records, alongside collaborations with artists including Vidna Obmana, Robert Rich and Jeffrey Fayman. Side-Line has covered Roach’s recent album and reissue activity, including “The Surface Below” and a reissue of “Stillpoint” (announced November 2025), the archival live collection “The Live Story” with Vidna Obmana (July 2025), a third vinyl edition of “Structures from Silence” (April 2025), and the live album “Crossing the Bridge” (January 2025). Roach also announced a limited 2CD, “La Rosa – Live in Tucson, 2025”, recorded at the same Tucson venue hosting Soundquest Festival this August. The Space Craft and Soundquest Festival dates place Roach on two of the more prominent ambient and electronic live bills of the 2026 season, continuing a year built around reissues, archival releases and festival appearances.

items.body: Lord Of The Lost will reissue “Empyrean” on 18 September 2026 through Out Of Line, marking the tenth anniversary of the German gothic-industrial metal band’s original album. This is a reissue of the 2016 record, not a new studio release. The 10th anniversary edition arrives in two formats. The limited 2LP edition (catalog OUT1551-1552) presses all 13 original tracks in a new remaster onto silver vinyl and adds the bonus track “One World, No Future,” originally released on the “Ruins” EP, a 2018 Sonic Seducer magazine exclusive. The 3CD edition (catalog OUT1548-1550) keeps the original album on disc one and adds two bonus discs: disc two collects rare cuts and alternate versions, including the fan-club-only track “One In A Million,” versions recorded during the COVID-19 lockdown era, a piano version, and one previously unreleased track; disc three carries 12 “Headphone 3D Mixes” of the album’s songs. “Empyrean” was originally released on 29 July 2016 through Out Of Line (catalog OUT 823), the band’s second concept album following “Antagony.” It reached number 9 on the German album charts and was the last Lord Of The Lost studio album released before the band signed to Napalm Records for 2018’s “Judgement.” Out Of Line describes the album’s sound as gothic metal colliding with glam, electro, prog and industrial elements, built around a dystopian, science-fiction narrative about humanity’s search for a promised world called Empyrean. The remastered album tracklist is: Miss Machine Drag Me to Hell The Love of God Raining Stars In Silence Black Oxide (feat. Scarlet Dorn) Interstellar Wars Doomsday Disco Death Penalty No Gods, No War The Interplay of Life and Death Utopya Where Is All the Love One World, No Future (bonus track) Side-Line reviewed “Empyrean” on its original release, praising the album’s mix of heavy guitar work, orchestral arrangements and Chris Harms‘ vocals, and singling out “Miss Machine,” “Doomsday Disco,” “No Gods, No War,” “The Interplay Of Life And Death” and “Utopya” as highlights. The band previously marked another album’s 10th anniversary in 2021 with a reissue of “Antagony,” its 2011 concept album. Lord Of The Lost ‘Empyrean’ bonus material and formats The “Ruins” EP track “One World, No Future,” now added to the 2LP, was originally limited to a Sonic Seducer magazine exclusive release in 2018. The 3CD edition’s second disc gathers material recorded across the album’s touring cycle, including the fan-club track “One In A Million” and lockdown-era recordings, alongside a piano version and one song that has not previously been released. Its third disc applies 12 “Headphone 3D Mixes” to the album’s tracks. About Lord Of The Lost Chris Harms founded Lord Of The Lost in Hamburg, Germany, in mid-2007 as a solo project before recruiting musicians from the city’s music scene to perform the songs live. The band released its debut single, “Dry the Rain,” in 2009, followed by its debut album, “Fears,” in February 2010 through Out Of Line. The second album, “Antagony,” followed in 2011 as the band’s first concept album, and “Die Tomorrow” arrived in 2012. Drummer Tobias Mertens joined in 2014, the same year the band completed its first US tour. In March 2015, Lord Of The Lost released the acoustic album “Swan Songs,” which reached number 34 on the German charts, followed later that year by the “Full Metal Whore” EP. “Empyrean,” the band’s second concept album, followed on 29 July 2016 through Out Of Line, preceded by the single “The Love of God” and the band’s first major European tour, alongside Combichrist and Filter. Guitarist Pi Stoffers and drummer Niklas Kahl joined in 2017, the year the band toured the UK with KMFDM. Lord Of The Lost signed to Napalm Records for 2018’s “Judgement,” continuing with “Judas” (2021), “Weapons of Mass Seduction” (2023) and the “OPVS NOIR” album trilogy released across 2025 and 2026. The band supported Iron Maiden across European tour legs in 2022 and 2023, and represented Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest 2023 with “Blood & Glitter.” The 10th anniversary reissue of “Empyrean” revisits the album that closed out the band’s independent Out Of Line era before its move to Napalm Records.

items.body: Berlin Banter‘s “Indistinct Chatter EP” is now available on green and white vinyl through Instant Noise Productions. The six-track release, which mixes trip hop, electropop and cinematic atmospheres, first came out digitally on May 2, 2025 through the same Berlin-based label. Most of the EP’s tracks are produced and mixed by Mark Saunders, whose credits include mixing work for The Cure and production and mixing work on Tricky’s 1995 debut album “Maxinquaye,” alongside credits for Erasure and a-ha. The track “I Shall Use My Time” features Mark Reeder, the Berlin-based British musician and producer who has lived in the city since 1978 and served as Factory Records’ de facto representative there before founding the electronic label MFS in 1990. “Crystalline” and “Clockwork Orange” both feature Simonne Jones, who sang on Sneaker Pimps‘ 2021 album “Squaring the Circle.” “People Will Unite” features Berlin hip hop artist Yaneq. The EP’s featured single, “I’ll Wait,” brings in Tricky, the Bristol trip hop artist born Adrian Thaws, and is mixed by Gareth Jones, the producer who worked on Depeche Mode’s “Construction Time Again,” “Some Great Reward” and “Black Celebration.” Side-Line previously covered the single’s release in a 2023 article. About Berlin Banter Berlin Banter is an electronic project introduced in 2021 with the five-track cover EP “All Too Familiar,” which reworked tracks by Yazoo, Depeche Mode, The Cure, Pet Shop Boys and Tanita Tikaram. The project returned in 2023 with the original single “I’ll Wait,” featuring Tricky and mixed by Gareth Jones. Berlin Banter released “Indistinct Chatter EP” digitally on May 2, 2025 through Instant Noise Productions, with production and mixing on most tracks by Mark Saunders and collaborations spanning Tricky, Simonne Jones, Mark Reeder and Yaneq. The EP is now also available on green and white vinyl through the label.

items.body: Glasszone, the coldwave project from Orléans, France, released the four-track EP “Lights” on May 16, 2026. The EP is available on Bandcamp, Spotify, Deezer, iTunes, Amazon Music and YouTube Music. Lights by Glasszone “Lights” runs four tracks: “Lights”, “The Void’s Echo”, “A Strange Feeling” and “Pictures”, all written by Glasszone. The EP carries the coldwave, gothic rock, deathrock, post-punk and shoegaze tags. On the release, Glasszone describes the setting as the misty banks of the Loire, where the project explores a dark and melodic coldwave built from incisive guitars, heavy rhythms and low vocals, moving between melancholy and a quiet tension. Glasszone’s ‘Lights’ EP continues a coldwave catalogue rooted in the Loire The four songs on “Lights” keep to the icy, hypnotic register that has defined Glasszone’s catalogue since its debut, pairing sharp guitar lines with heavier rhythm parts and deep, restrained vocals. About Glasszone Glasszone is a coldwave and post-punk project founded in 2017 in Orléans, on the Loire river in France, self-released and drawing on 80s coldwave with The Cure, Christian Death, Joy Division, Mephisto Walz and Cocteau Twins among its reference points. The project also records as Ex Visio and has issued ten releases between 2018 and 2023, including the albums “Garden of Glass”, “The Other Side”, “Another Dark Place”, “Restless Nights”, “Sleeping Flowers”, “Pictures of the Past”, “Moments” and “To Leave Behind”. “Lights” is Glasszone’s latest EP, released digitally on May 16, 2026.

The video, shot in the high desert, is out now on the band’s own channels. Mellow Code is led by Josh McVety and Oliver Michael German. McVety appears throughout, intercut with scenes shot from inside a van. McVety, who also works as a carpenter and fabricator, describes the shoot as a collaboration with his own circle of artists: “This video was an absolute labor of love that was entirely done with and by my community of artist friends.
